speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to have tabled today the reports of the study teams of the task force on program review. The volumes that I have tabled represent the combined efforts of 221 individual Canadians who have reviewed nearly 1,000 programs and services in the federal Government. Perhaps that is some explanation for the hon. gentleman.
Over half of the men and women who were involved in the work of the study teams were recruited from the private sector. These men and women came from Victoria to St. John's, left their jobs and their families to serve their country without remuneration, each for three months. Among those who so served were senior executives of major corporations and small businesses, labour leaders, city administrators, and provincial deputies. I want to take this opportunity to formally recognize the debt of gratitude the Government and the country owe these outstanding Canadians.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext:
Like the review itself, the output of these individuals is unique in the annals of Canadian public administration. Never before has there been such a broad representation from outside Government in such a wide-ranging examination. The release of the work of these mixed study teams is a public acknowledgement of their extraordinarily valuable contribution. Each study team reviewed the array of programs within their area of examination and prepared assessment notes on each program, presenting options for improvement and reform. In addition, the study teams prepared thematic overviews to describe their over-all assessment of program groupings. These study team reports were then referred to the Private Sector Advisory Committee comprising 12 representatives of labour, business, and professional organizations. The organizations themselves selected the representatives of their respective organizations to serve on that Committee. I would like to acknowledge these individuals and their sponsoring organizations for their outstanding leadership during the past year.
This private sector advisory committee met every Monday throughout the year-long course of program review and acted as a further review mechanism to the work coming to it from the 19 individual study teams. The study team reports I have just tabled today are the final product of this process of consultation and co-operation. Philip Aspinall, Chairman of

March 11, 1986
Statements by Ministers
the Private Sector Advisory Committee, and Darcy McKeough, the Private Sector Liaison Advisor, will be meeting the media shortly to describe in more detail the work of the study teams. I would, however, like to take a few minutes to highlight some of the major observations of this work.
The Government of Canada has for decades been functioning in a twilight of partial information, overlapping responsibilities, and organizational inefficiencies. This condition has allowed structural distortions to creep into our economy and our society. Canadians deserve to know more about the myriad of programs and services they pay for. After a little over a year of careful examination by mixed teams of private and public-sector analysts, we know much more than any Government has ever known before.
This Government is not the first to discover the necessity for a wide-ranging, unfettered and objective analysis of the federal public administration. Over the years a number of studies, including the Glassco Commission and the Lambert Commission, described this situation. Several years ago the Auditor-General concluded that the management of Government was "out of control". During the summer election campaign of 1984, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), who was then Prime Minister, recognized the dimensions of the problem when he said:
There is a lot of space to reduce and cut expenditures and duplications: programs which are no longer in force, which are no longer pertinent, wastages in public administration.
[ Translation]
What is unique in this case is that a party newly in power took advantage of this opportunity to open the doors and conduct an independent analysis in co-operation with the private sector. In other words, to welcome new ideas. And today, by publishing the conclusions of the study teams, we are opening those doors even wider.
A central conclusion of the study teams, and one with potentially profound implications, is the degree to which there has developed a vast array of government programs that are designed to subsidize activity rather than results, effort rather than success. Few who take the time and spend the effort to read the study team reports could dispute the observation that we have become a nation of what I call program junkies. In the absence of a full comprehension of the extent, nature and content of government programs, past Governments have felt little reluctance to use subsidies as a blanket solution to many problems of society. Therefore, government spending, including tax expenditures, has been expanding with the inexorable growth of a rolling snowball.
As I have said, the implications are profound, for the analysis I have just described reflects how dependent on government Canadians have become. The elements of this conclusion were evident from the first study team report, when those examining business services and subsidies observed that
the Government has been "giving with both hands". However, it was important to await the observations of all the study teams before coming to any over-all conclusion.
My decision as chairman of the task force was not to pre-empt or to prejudice the work of study teams by releasing reports throughout the year. For this reason, I felt it was desirable that the reports be published together.
The study team reports and their options represent the first orderly step toward cabinet discussion. They do not represent government policy nor are they decisions of the Government. The reports provide the basis for discussion of the wide array of programs which exist throughout government and provide a valuable tool in the decision-making process.
Having said that, it is obvious from announcements already made throughout the past year that the business of governing has proceeded responsibly, while the review has been underway.
The decisions that have already flowed from the process of program review are of the following nature.
Decisions have been made on programs and services where the focus is primarily on the internal administration of federal Departments and agencies. Examples are in the area of regulatory reform, real property management and veterans' programs. In addition, a limited number of decisions have been made with implications for the provinces. These were in areas largely where we had confidence from our continuing federal-provincial consultations that the provincial Governments concurred with our direction. Examples include the Canada Assistance Plan and housing programs and devolution to the provinces in small cases under DRIE's Industrial and Regional Development Program.
On behalf of the Prime Minister, I have given written assurance to the provinces that no unilateral decisions will be taken by the federal Government and that advance consultation will occur before federal programs are revamped in ways that affect the provinces-especially where provincial Governments share program costs.
It should be noted that in making decisions the federal Government has not, and will not, be bound just to the options put forward by the study teams. A close reading of these reports will show that independent study teams, working within their individual terms of reference and examining the same programs, can come to different and sometimes contradictory conclusions. This only confirms the autonomy of individual study teams.
While the Government will be taking the options presented by these mixed study teams into account, it must and will make its decisions from a perspective that is broader than that of any individual study team.
Finally, the Government is referring these reports to the respective Standing Committees so that their analyses and their options can be assessed in the light of open public discussion. This Government is committed to parliamentary reform and determined that parliamentarians become meaningfully involved in the broader reforms to public policy.
March 11, 1986

The process of program review and the reports I have tabled today are steps in the reform of public administration in Canada. Parliamentary reform relates to the way decisions are made by elected officials. We must join these reform initiatives to policy-making in Canada.
Sir, the Government has been asking Canadians to join our commitment to the reform of Government as part of the mandate for economic renewal given to us by the people of Canada in September, 1984. The tabling of these documents shows beyond any reasonable doubt that this Government remains committed to policies of economic renewal in a climate of openness and public dialogue. We are committed to improving the management of Government and providing better service to the public.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Order, please.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all we want to congratulate the participants who worked on these reports, a great many of them voluntarily, and we appreciate the amount of time that they have spent composing these reports for consideration by the Government of Canada and by this House. We are sure that the good things in the reports will be ignored by the Government, and certainly the cuts that have been suggested will certainly be implemented by the Government of Canada. This Government is more interested in figures than it is people. This Government is more interested in cuts. They have an obsession with cuts and reducing services to Canadians.
Perhaps the first thing that one will note in looking at some of these reports is that the Government of Canada really did not wait for these studies to be done. If one just peruses some of the reports, for example, the one on housing he will find that it deals with the RRAP program. One section deals with the Canadian Oil Substitution Program. Another section deals with the Home Heating Oil Subsidy Program and exemptions for CHIP grants in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. Canadians and Members of the House know that these programs have been terminated since these study groups began.
We can look at another report on the environment. We see sections dealing with national parks and the weather services. There is a magnificent section dealing with the wildlife conservation programs, including migratory birds conservation, wildlife research and conservation and wildlife interpretation. After this study group began to study these programs the Government decimated the Canadian Wildlife Service.
We can go on to look at another report on major surveys, including the Surveys and Mapping Branch, the Canadian hydrographic service and oceanographic data. The list goes on. We know what the Government has done since these study groups began their work. We know about the charges it has implemented that make it practically impossible for people in the fishery to even buy charts.
Statements by Ministers
Let us go on to look at job creation, training and employment services. That is an interesting report which studies Canada Works. We all know that Canada Works is no longer in existence. This report studied Katimavik and many other programs which have been dealt with by the Government since the study groups began their work. Yet the Minister stands up in the House to say that the Government will not unilaterally make any changes in the Government until this report has been studied by the Standing Committees of the House and reported to the Canadian people.
We are also concerned about what interpretation the Government will give to the positive conclusions that were arrived at because of a sincere concern on the part of the participants in these study groups. We need only to go back to when the Minister presented his reports from the study teams in May, 1985 to understand the basis for our concern. In that report of the various study groups we can see some constructive comments under targeting of scientific research and development through the National Research Council, but we know what the Government of Canada did to the National Research Council following the presentation of that report.
When we look at the employment services section of that report that was presented last May and look under "job placement", we know that the Government cut out the mobility grants that were available to Canadians in order to move from one part of the country to the other. The Government took the main representations of those study groups on training, job creation and employment programs at face value and reorganized the direct job creation delivery of programs in this country. But did the Government consult with those who were affected-the unemployed? No. It commissioned some fine studies to be conducted by very educated people from the universities, the trade schools and the unions as well as private enterprise. It then discontinued the direct job creation programs for the poor man with a family and only eight weeks of work in a year. Those individuals are not allowed to work under direct job-creation programs of the Government because of the interpretation given to the recommendations of that particular study group.
According to the Government's largest employment program, a person who has trained in the occupation of a job being advertised cannot be referred to that job. For instance, an unemployed carpenter is not allowed to be referred to a carpentry job in his community. A person who has just finished a carpentry course in trade school is not allowed to be referred to that job. The Government has proven that grave errors are made when the people affected by these reports are not consulted.
In conclusion, we want to congratulate the people who formulated these reports. We look forward to examining the reports and holding the Government accountable for its actions. The Government should not proceed with any further changes to our system until there has been full consultation, not only in this chamber but with the people in our society who are affected by those changes.

March 11, 1986
Statements by Ministers

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in commenting on the Task Force reports which we received about an hour ago, I was tempted to bring all the documents with me and ask whether there is an agenda for action by the Conservative Government, or whether it intends to pick and choose which of those recommendations it finds most to its favour. In fact, when I look through the document, I begin to see that this is simply a continuation of what we have seen from the Government in its First 18 months in office. The values of Bay Street and Wall Street prevail in the Government's budgetary policy as well as in the Nielsen Task Force review which has been brought forward today.
It is quite clear that the unfairness that led to a $1,300 increase in taxes on the average family between the November, 1984 statement, the May, 1985 Budget and the most recent Budget is to continue. When it comes to spending review, or program review as the Government calls it, it intends to take away essential services to ordinary Canadians while leaving the services to the business and corporate sector essentially untouched, unexamined and in fact uncut.
In effect, the other shoe has dropped. We see that the unfairness of the tax policy is being matched by the unfairness in terms of spending policy. The Government began the Nielsen Task Force by saying that the goal was to eliminate waste and inefficiency in Government. What we are in fact seeing is that the Government intends to eliminate services that are extremely important to average Canadians.
In order to conduct this review the Government spent much money and invited 221 experts from different walks of public and private life to meet every week. The Deputy Primer Minister (Mr. Nielsen) has given his praise for their work. Rather than suggesting that the Government is grossly inefficient or wasteful, that study group suggested a number of areas to be cut and chopped. The sections of the report that I have read indicate that the group frequently agrees with the priorities, prejudices and biases of the Progressive Conservative Government. Perhaps they were chosen to conduct this review for precisely that reason.
The House Leader feels somewhat aggrieved by that, but I do not remember, from my experience in the Ontario Legislature, that Darcy McKeough was particularly concerned about the needs of ordinary Ontarians. Yet he has played a key role in sifting through the recommendations of the various study groups.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

There was one member of the review committee and he was there to try to prevent some of the worst things from happening. If you put one trade unionist with eleven people on the main review committee and you have 200 people from the private sector, you end up with the introduction that we see.
The first substantive recommendation in this report deals with the question of universality. It says that as far as the Task Force is concerned it found universality everywhere it looked and it is determined to stamp that out. It intends to take away
universality. We debated the principle of universality in 1984 and 1985. Those debates took place because ordinary Canadians were very concerned about the fact that the Government was backing away from universal programs that were essential to the average Canadian family. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stood in his place to say that universality was a sacred trust. The sacred trust means, obviously, it was to be defended for at least 12 months before the program review came in. Now we have this new attack on universality which appears will mark this Government up until the next election.
We are told that study team after study team focused on universal subsidy programs and then built a case to abolish them. I am not sure whether or not what is in this report is Government policy. We are told it is not. But yesterday I received a phone call from the Public Service Staff Relations Board and was told that 15 workers in one particular section had been given pink slips and were told they were being fired because of the Nielsen Task Force. The task force report is not Government policy until the Government decides to make a move, and it would appear it does not particularly want to have a process of public review over a series of recommendations which, to put it mildly, vary a great deal in terms of quality.
The documents point to the lack of control over tax expenditures as a major weakness in Government financial accountability. I welcome that admission. The documents confirm the estimates of the Auditor General of between $30 billion to $50 billion in tax expenditure taking place every year, and that this is an area of Government expenditure which is essentially not under control. Neither the Liberals nor the Progressive Conservatives have shown themselves to be accountable in this particular area.
My hopes with the introduction of the document were that perhaps the review would deal substantively with the question of tax expenditures. My hopes have been dashed, however, as I look at what has been done in terms of tax expenditures to business. When we get down to the specific recommendations, we Find that the task force has copped out when it comes to dealing with major tax expenditures to business and to the wealthy. The largest tax expenditure that I can see in this particular document is the accelerated depreciation which is given to business. In spite of all of the resources of the task force, it was unable to come up with an estimate of the value of that particular tax expenditure more recent than 1981. If that tax expenditure was worth about $3 billion in 1981, one has to assume that in 1986-87 it will be worth between $5 billion and $6 billion. How does the task force deal with that major expenditure? Did it really go into it in order to see whether it was justified or whether there were better ways of spending the public funds of the taxpayers? No, it did not. It stated that while it was most difficult for the Department of Finance to evaluate, its impression, based on discussions with the Department of Finance, is that it believes that the objectives of the system of tax expenditures for accelerated depreciation are reasonably satisFied.
March 11, 1986

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext: Spoken like a bunch of corporate giants.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER-STUDY TEAM REPORTS
speechtext:
That is right, Mr. Speaker. What it did when it assessed various programs of tax expenditures to the corporate sector was to adopt the principle of revenue neutrality. Even if it thought that in certain cases some reductions in tax expenditures should be made, rather than saying, "Let us ensure that the money goes into the hands of the taxpayers and is used for other purposes", it said, "But if we take those tax expenditures away, we should reduce the over-all tax rate so business in general is not left to be suffering at all".
That is particularly objectionable, given the statistics which indicate that the corporate sector in Canada now takes more from Government in terms of grants and tax expenditures than it pays in corporation taxes. In 1983-which are the latest figures we were able to get, lacking the ample resources available to the Nielsen Task Force-corporations paid about $7 billion in taxes and received $12 billion in tax subsidies and grants. That is a far cry from the ordinary family who were seeing their taxes go up by $1,300 per annum as a consequence of the tax measures of the Government, and the taxpayers know damn well they are paying a lot more than they are receiving from the Government.
There is something wrong with a task force which spends as much time in minuscule considerations of cuts in the patent office, recommendations which have already been demonstrated to be unworkable, to be based on faulty information and to be totally unsustainable and justifiable, as it does on a program which now costs $5 billion or $6 billion in terms of tax expenditures through the process of accelerated depreciation.
I want to suggest that even a cursory glance at these documents suggest that they are widely varying in quality and in terms of the degree to which the very study teams accepted what they were told by the Government, the degree to which they accepted the line they received from the Government. The quality is enormously variable; the prejudices, however, are consistent. Those prejudices, I want to reiterate.

Those prejudices come from St. James Street, from Bay Street and from Wall Street in New York. It means that instead of a study of Government spending that focuses on the interests of the average Canadian family, of the people on Main Street, Canada, we have a study containing 21 papers, all of which reflect this Government's bias towards the corporate sector, the big companies and the rich in our society who ignore the needs of the average family and small business people in this country.

I would like to give an example of the prejudices found in this particular report. Universality is the first target. If we accept the task force, I suspect there will be no more universal programs. The task force recommends the elimination of most non-profit and co-operative housing programs. It recommends that employable people now receiving welfare be moved over to unemployment insurance, apparently to save tax dollars.
Statements by Ministers
And when the unemployment insurance benefits run out 1 suppose they will have to take their tin cup to Sparks Street or to Bay Street and hope that they can survive on that. The task force proposes that the Government withdraw from native health services. In the area of regional development it proposes to eliminate the subsidies for marine transportation even where that is vital to keeping our country together. It proposes that subsidies in grain movement will go to farmers, not the railways, something which was fought bitterly in this House over the course of the two or three years before 1984. Despite the promises made during the election campaign by the Progressive Conservative Party, the task force recommends an end to all farm fuel tax rebates. It is recommending that one of the important programs for the maintenance of cash flow for farmers, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments program, be cancelled. It is proposing to eliminate all socio-economic considerations for the fisheries as well as the federal role in habitat protection in western Canada. It is proposing to reduce expenditures in person years in fisheries by 20 per cent in two years. It is proposing what is said to be aggressive cost recovery on coastguards, harbours and so on, which I suspect would lead to our coasts becoming depopulated because no one would be able to afford to use the harbours.
One would assume that perhaps the task force would recommend means of increasing employment, but one does not increase employment by terminating Katimavik, as the task force recommended, which has led now to the tragic events taking place outside of the Senate. The founder of Katimavik is now engaging in a hunger strike. The task force is proposing that training spending be cut to 95 per cent of 1985 levels. It suggests that future guaranteed training levels be eliminated, that critical trades skills training be cut in half, and that the basic adult literacy program be eliminated. These are just a few of the recommendations of the Nielsen Task Force. It is proposing that the Canada Council be made a flagship for grants and, as a consequence, that other programs of support for cultural activities be cut, and is proposing to freeze the capital budget of the CBC. It is considering the elimination of the National Film Board because "it is a threat to the private film sector in Canada". It proposes to cut women's programs to the levels of 1983-1984.
It is proposing to look at the whole system of exemptions on sales tax and to raise the sales tax on building materials, bicycles, non-prescription drugs, clothing and a number of other items. That is again a somewhat mindless approach. [Translation]
-once more, I suggest that this list may be satisfactory to the people on Bay Street, on St. James Street and on Wall Street, but it will not satisfy the people on Main Street. It will certainly not satisfy the people on average incomes, the middle income families in Canada.

This is a shopping list for Bay Street at the expense of Main
Street. In conclusion, I do welcome the fact that the Government intends to refer this matter to the various standing

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mclnnes that Bill C-87, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to speak to Bill C-87, which is entitled "an Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof'. The long and short of this particular Bill is that the Government is asking the House of Commons to authorize it to sell a Crown corporation, Canadians Arsenals Limited, and to place that company into private hands.
Taken within the context of the way the Government is behaving with respect to all social, cultural and trade policies, this is one more piece of evidence which convinces us that the Government is again being irresponsible and amoral-in fact, in this case it convinces us that this is an immoral Government. We are told that the purchaser is the SNC group of Montreal, Quebec, which has operations in that province. I hasten to say that I have absolutely nothing of a negative nature to say about SNC. This is not a question of whether or not we are concerned and in favour of this particular company buying Canadian Arsenals Limited over and above some other company. Indeed, I was pleased to read in the release made by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes) that 500 of the 4,000 employees of that company own the plant and the corporation. In that sense it is an enlightened company, if that number of employees are shareholders in it. I hope no one will regard my comments with respect to what the Government is doing in selling this corporation off as being in any way aimed at SNC.
My Liberal colleagues have expressed in their speeches so far in the House-and I trust they will in the future-their objections to the sale and a number of technical factors involved with it. For example, they are concerned about the sale price. We are told that the report commissioned on behalf of the Government by Arthur Andersen states that the value of the company is between $80 million and $98 million. Some of my colleagues have been asking whether or not this sale price of $92 million is an adequate price. They point out that, after all, the assets were alleged to be worth $126 million in 1984. Apparently business is booming at Canadian Arsenals Limited. Its profit levels have gone up constantly year after year. My colleagues are wondering if this sale price is a good one or if this is another fire sale like de Havilland. They also say that they cannot really know. We in Parliament are being asked, as in the case of de Havilland, to give our support to something without having the facts at hand.
A Government that came to office claiming that it was going to enforce freedom of information is apparently unwilling to disclose to these representatives of the Canadian people in the House of Commons the figures and the report from Arthur Anderson. Apparently we are asked to simply proceed on faith, as we were asked to do so in the $1 billion giveaway to the banks and in the de Havilland case.
Of course, the Government realized later on that people of Canada really do not approve of these hidden, secretive methods of selling off things that belong to the Canadian people, or giving away money without giving the Canadian people and opportunity to have access to it. One would think that the Government would have learned. It has had to back off time after time and finally give in and give to the people of Canada the information they have demanded. That was true with the banks, and especially true with de Havilland. There are objections from my colleagues that they are not in a position to be able to make a competent judgment on behalf of their con-
March 11, 1986

stituents and the Canadian people with regard to the value of this particular sale.
Some of my colleagues have pointed out that there is also a problem in that this may create a monopoly situation. They feel that the Government is providing a company an opportunity to have monopoly access to the Canadian Government for the selling of ammunition. They feel that this sale to the Canadian Government could then be boosted to whatever price the company might wish. There is no clear explanation as to how this might be avoided if this company is put into the hands of a private-sector firm.
As well, some of my colleagues are concerned about the fact that the Public Service Alliance, despite all the claims of the Tories that they are going to consult, has not been consulted. The Tories have again made a mockery of this statement in presenting the Nielsen report. They say they consult the Canadian people when they in fact act first and consult afterward.
My colleagues point out that the Public Service Alliance indicates that the workers at Canadian Arsenals Limited were not consulted. Despite the comments of the NDP indicating that there was no concern given by the Government to the pensions of the workers at Canadian Arsenals Limited, I was glad to see that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes) had indeed taken some steps to protect the interests of the workers at least by way of pensions, and I commend him for that effort.
While there has been Government secrecy, a lack of consultation and the fact that once again the Government is selling out a profitable Crown corporation which belongs to the taxpayers at fire sale prices, I have other reservations about this particular sale. I have additional objections to this sale on the grounds that all this in any case fits into a most regrettable over-all Tory approach, which is that the only way to measure what we do is to get money for it. Making money and saving money are the considerations of the Government first, second and last. The consequence of this kind of approach to governing is to destroy life, to destroy the quality of life or to destroy our environment for the sake of a fast buck. I suggest that this Government's over-all approach to young people, senior citizens and those groups that are aggrieved, including the poor, is that it cares about statistics, not people. It cares about statistics instead of people.
In selling off the ammunition company to the private sector, the Government is encouraging this company to compete for contracts abroad. That is my indictment of this deal. This company will be put into the private sector and there is nothing to keep us from seeing this organization fall into the hands of some organization other than SNC, an organization that will sell ammunition for profit. In fact, the Government admits this and boasts about it. The Government points out that this new consortium will be better able to compete in the international markets. After all, SNC only makes small ammunition but will now be able to get into the business of large ammunition and in fact create a much larger complex which can compete more effectively on the international mar-
Canadian Arsenals Limited
kets. That is a tragic confession on the part of the Government. Is that not just what we would expect of the Tories? They do not mind Canada being a merchant of death if it will turn a buck.
This is the case not only for this one sale. On the contrary, this fits into the Conservatives' total philosophy. The Minister of Supply and Services was selling off for a fast buck a Canadian Crown corporation to a non-Canadian company. We saw this approach in the case of de Havilland. But the most shocking and callous example of all was the recent announcement by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) that he would solve the economic problems of Cape Breton by bringing to Cape Breton an ammunitions plant. Is that the way to solve the economic problems on a long-term basis? An ammunitions plant in Cape Breton will have to do whatever it can to turn a buck. Of course, if it is in Cape Breton, it is able to sell from Canada in a way that it cannot sell from its own country.
Which company was this that the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion suggested would set up a plant in Cape Breton to help Cape Bretoners with their economic problems? It was suggested that the company that would come to Cape Breton to make machines of war would be the Thissen Company. Thissen is the name of the father, if you will, of the Nazi war machine. Thissen was the man who originally put Hitler into business and who financed his campaign and armed his bully thugs. Thissen was the man who set up the armaments machine of the Nazi Wehrmacht. That was Thissen. Imagine suggesting that a company with that name could come to Cape Breton to set up an armaments plant in order to be merchants of war and sell to whomever will buy. It is disgusting. It is a revolting thought. It is insensitive and it is criminal.
Is the way to solve the economic problems of Canadian people to make us merchants of war?
It is the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion who suggested this solution to the problems of Cape Breton. 1 am concerned that this can be done without the blinking of an eye, without some concern on the part of the Government which did not deny this but is rather considering this as a way to solve our problems
Is it not true that for decades Canada has built its reputation upon being a country of peace? Is it not true that we have indicated repeatedly that we would not be merchants of war or merchants of death? Is it not true that Canada has indicated that it would not sell armaments throughout the world to countries which use them to destroy one another, to kill one another? Is it not true that we do not want to be contributors to more bloodshed in the Middle East, Africa and Asia?
Canada is not in the business of selling armaments in order to make our living in the world. We can find better and more constructive ways, by setting up companies which deal in the fields of environmental, medical, biochemical, and biomedical research. We have enough brains in Canada to concentrate on things that build rather than on things that destroy.

March 11, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
I have a concern about the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited. It is one small, miniscule part of a total approach in a program which is insensitive about matters of war and peace, and about how Canada images itself in the world. Canada plays its role to bring about peace in a world weary of war, where millions of people are starving, suffering and dying. Do we need to become involved in the munitions business and send out weapons for people to kill one another? Is that what Canada is to become? I do not care which administration would do it or did it. I do not care what Party label is on it. I am saying that it is not good now. We should not approve of this kind of approach to solving our economic problems. It is better that the company remain in the hands of the Government and not become part of an arsenal of machinery or of an industrial military complex.
When Dwight D. Eisenhower became President of the United States, he confessed that he was concerned that the United States was doomed and had been sold out to the industrial military complex which was calling the shots for him in the White House. He expressed dismay and concern. We do not want to build our economy on any kind of industrial military complex. Perhaps the Tories emulate and look with great satisfaction at how the United States has built up a $2.5 trillion deficit, mainly on defence, mainly on the largest machinery of war ever created in the history of the human race. That is what the Americans base their budget on, going to defence, as they call it. Is that how we will build up the Canadian economy? Are we envious of the Americans? Do we want to get into the business with them? Are we so hungry for profits that that is the direction in which we have to turn? I do not think a single Canadian would say yes to that.
The people of Prince Edward Island are concerned that Litton Systems might come there; that is becoming a problem in that province. Canadians do not feel that they want to make money from the blood on the faces of other men. That has been a Canadian sense of pride throughout our history. We have only gone to war to destroy oppression. We have not fed the machines of war and we have not profited from it. I am sure that those whose sons died in the last war to put down Hitler will not appreciate the fact that we are considering bringing Thissen into Canada to sell munitions and to profit. That company was founded by the men who backed and put Hitler into power.
Canada should be perceived as a messenger of peace. Therefore I believe that we should reconsider all steps, not only the one which we are considering now, which is a little one in the over-all issue. I plead with the Conservative Government to re-examine its priorities. Above all it should give support to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). If he is to go throughout the world saying that Canada stands for peace, we should not be making Canada appear to be a merchant of war.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on Bill C-87, an Act to sell Canadian Arsenals Limited to the private sector. Some people may ask the following questions. What is Canadian Arsenals Limited,
how important is it, and why should it not be sold to the private sector? We have heard a few speeches in the House outlining the whole theory of why we should be selling arms at all, and why we should be privatizing a somewhat important Canadian Crown corporation which will now probably go out to peddle arms around the world. I find that to be morally repugnant. It is the main reason I oppose the sale of the particular Crown corporation to the private sector.
The reason the Government is selling this particular Crown corporation is nothing short of its dogmatic commitment to the ideology of privatization.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) can rise to contradict those comments with good arguments. I invite her to do so. Canadian Arsenals is a very profitable Crown corporation. It has a lot of money. It has a lot of guaranteed contracts. From a business point of view, it is a sound business corporation which has made a lot of dough. Why get rid of it? Why not keep the corporation and use its profits to reduce the deficit? It does not make any sense whatsoever to sell it.
Canadian Arsenals Limited was founded back in 1945. It is owned 100 per cent by the people of the country through the federal Government of Canada. It manufactures medium and large calibre ammunition. Its main customer for 90 per cent of its production is the Department of National Defence. The Government is selling a Crown corporation which sells 90 per cent of its products to the Government itself. I ask whether that makes any sense. It is an industry which is located entirely in the Province of Quebec. It has two plants. One is located in St. Augustin just outside Quebec City. The second is in Le Gardeur just outside Montreal. As I said, the company has been very profitable. Ninety per cent of its production is sold to the federal Government of Canada and 10 per cent of its production is exported. It has many contracts. However, the Government of Canada wants to sell it. I really wonder why, other than its dogmatic commitment to the ideology of privatization. We can see what that has done for Margaret Thatcher in Britain.
The employees of the company are organized by the Public Service Alliance of Canada. It is my understanding that the union was not consulted on the sale at all. Its workers are concerned about their pension benefits. There is no guarantee about jobs or job security. Suddenly the Minister announced that the company would be sold, and that was it.
I should like to refer to a press release issued on December 2, 1985 by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) who is also in charge of the privatization task force. He said: "Currently the government of Canada purchases 90 per cent of Canadian Arsenals Limited's production. This Crown corporation, CAL, has been impeded in exploring opportunities to diversify". The Minister is saying that because it is a Crown corporation it has not had the chance to diversify as it might be able to do in the private sector. He went on to say: "The Government is confident that once the company is
March 11, 1986

privatized, CAL will produce additional markets in product diversification. Indeed, through this sale, the Canadian ammunition industry should become internationally competitive, making possible increased sales to our NATO partners".
One of the purposes of the sale is to try to make Canadian Arsenals Limited a merchant of war peddling arms around the world. 1 ask Conservative Members of Parliament whether or not this is really what they want. Here we have a Cabinet Minister saying that if we sell this company it will pursue additional markets around the world. It will diversify its products, selling to God knows whom, Mr. Speaker, in different parts of the world. I say to you, Sir, that this country has had a very proud record of not being a merchant of war and it has had a very proud record of not creating jobs through producing bombs, rifles and ammunition. That has been neither our history nor our tradition. Going back 50 or 60 years, it was not our tradition. It was not our tradition in the Pearson years, the Diefenbaker years, the Trudeau years or in the Clark era.
Why do we have this change in policy? Why is the new Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) privatizing a very profitable company? One of the major purposes being to diversify and pursue international markets so as to peddle guns. That is not good enough. I wish for once that some of the backbench Conservative Members of Parliament would get up and say what they feel and think, and say no to the Prime Minister who is trying to change Canadian foreign policy in this very important way. Why is he doing it?
SNC Defence Products of Montreal is a private company that produces ammunition. Is the Government selling CAL to SNC in Montreal because that company contributes money to the Conservative Party for electoral purposes?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: That is silly.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
There we have a Member of Parliament from Alberta saying silly. I just happen to have here a copy of an article from The Toronto Sun. If the Member thinks this is foolish, he should get up and respond in a few minutes time. The Toronto Sun for Dec. 4, 1985 writes that SNC contributed $1,000 directly into the campaign funds of the Minister of Industry in his fight for re-election in his Toronto area riding in 1984. So we have a $1,000 contribution to the Minister's campaign fund.
Further, La Presse reports on February 19, 1986 that SNC contributed in excess of $10,000 to the Tory campaign in 1984. I ask my friend from Alberta whether it is silly to wonder why the sale of this private Crown corporation is going to SNC when it contributes money to the Tory campaign caucus. Here we have a private manufacturer of ammunition contributing to the Conservative Party. That same Conservative Party is privatizing Canadian Arsenals and selling it to SNC. Is there a bit of hanky-panky going on behind the scenes and that is why the Government is privatizing this company? I wonder.
Canadian Arsenals Limited
SNC has sold ammunition to the rebels in Nicaragua in the past. If it did that in the past, and if we in this House allow the privatization of Canadian Arsenals, then there is nothing to say that that company will not sell more ammunition to the rebels in Nicaragua who are trying to unseat the Sandanista Government. It is against the foreign policy of this country, as stated many times by the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina), to export arms of any sort to a trouble spot like that in the world.
Are we in this House being complicit in escalating a war in Nicaragua because we are selling Canadian Arsenals to the private sector? That is one question I would like to have answered by Conservative Members. I do know that there are some progressive Members in the Conservative Party who are concerned about President Reagan's push to fund the anti-Sandanista contras in Nicaragua with $100 million for arms and military equipment and who are concerned about the possibility of another Vietnam in Central America. Yet here we have a Canadian Conservative Government selling Canadian Arsenals Limited to a private firm that has sold ammunition to the rebels in Nicaragua. I think that is a very important moral question that Conservative Members of Parliament had better answer before we allow this Bill to become law.
I also mentioned that CAL has been very profitable in the last few years. It has made millions of dollars. Its projected sales and profits for the next few years will be about 20 per cent per year. I ask again, why sell a company that is so profitable? Why sell a company that does 90 per cent of its business with the Canadian Government? Why privatize a company of that sort, Mr. Speaker? It is one of Canada's most successful Canadian Crown corporations. I thought it was good business to keep things that are doing well. I thought the private enterprise philosophy said that if things are going well and you are making a profit, you keep it and reinvest the profits, but divest something that is not doing too well. So I ask why sell it?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Free enterprise.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member from Montreal says: it is free enterprise. But free enterprise for whom, Mr. Speaker? Is it free enterprise for war merchants?

Free enterprise for whom?
As I said before, 90 per cent of its market is guaranteed by the Department of National Defence. Why sell? Its sales are expected to double. It is Canada's third most profitable company, so why sell it unless you want to enhance the profits of some members of a private company that contributed to the Conservative Party? I see the Member from Camrose or Battle River. He is so excited that he is jumping to his feet. He is embarrassed by the sale of Canadian Arsenals. I will not go on too long because I know he wants to participate. He, being a red Tory, is embarrassed-

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Oh, oh!

March 11, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: -by this kind of blatant privatization to thicken the pocketbooks of contributors of the Conservative Party in the City of Montreal. I know that the successor to Jack Horner in this House must be repulsed by that very idea.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Stand up and be counted, Arnold.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
If the Member did not have a Prime Minister who would keep a tight reign on him he would be up in this House making a very eloquent plea that we should not be going ahead with this deal, in the tradition of John Diefenbaker who would never have done this kind of thing. John Diefenbaker would never have sold Canadian Arsenals to a company selling ammunition to Nicaragua and the rebels, escalating a war in a far-away land. I know that a red Tory like the Member from Central Alberta is very unhappy about this type of deal. I wish he would use his seniority and his muscle to teach the Prime Minister a few facts of Canadian life and tell him of some of the important things surrounding the history of our country and what it has stood for over the years.
I appeal to Members of the Conservative Party to not let the country become a merchant of death or a merchant of war. If this company is privatized and sold to SNC in the Province of Quebec, as the President of the Treasury Board said, the company will then pursue additional markets, diversify its products and sell internationally. But what is this company going to sell? Ammunition and guns. It is not selling food products or machinery and technology to the Third World countries to help them become self sufficient. The company is selling guns, just like President Reagan in the United States who is trying to sell guns to the rebels in Nicaragua. Thank goodness that members of the Congress and members of the Senate in the United States are saying no to Ronald Reagan.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: That is dirty.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
A Member of the Conservative Party says that is dirty. Of course, it is dirty work that Ronald Reagan is trying to do in Nicaragua. I agree. But the American Congress and the Senate will not let Ronald Reagan get away with it. Let us not do by the back door some of the President's dirty work in Canada by selling this Crown corporation to the private sector that will produce arms for Central America. It is a question of morality. It is something we should not be doing as a country.
It is also a question of good economic sense. Why sell a very profitable Crown corporation to the private sector? Why sell to the private sector a corporation which is doing very well? Please get up and respond to that. If something works well, the Conservative Party wants to get rid of it and load more and more debt on the shoulders of the people of Canada. If something is not going very well, they do not seem to have any response whatsoever. This is the same Conservative Party that puts tax after tax after tax on the farmers in my constituency. The same Conservative Party that in the Budget of a week or so ago got rid of the investment tax credit for farmers. That means a tax increase of $50 million a year for Saskatchewan
farmer, and some $150 million a year for all farmers, including those in Ontario who produce tobacco. If you increase the tax load of farmers by 50 per cent you are putting a lot of them out of business. At the same time they will line the pockets of their wealthy friends in Quebec, Ontario and elsewhere by selling them a very successful Canadian Crown corporation with a guaranteed 20 per cent return per year, and increased sales each and every year. It makes no sense whatsoever.
All we hear from this Government is taxes, taxes, taxes. Since the Conservatives took power in September, 1984, the average family in my riding has seen its federal taxes go up by $1,304 a year. The sales tax went up by 1 per cent in the last Budget, 1 per cent in the previous Budget, and 1 per cent in the financial statement of November, 1984. There was a 3 per cent increase in income taxes as well. The ordinary people in this country get taxes, taxes, taxes. The wealthy people of this country get all kinds of tax breaks so they can line their pockets with extra money.
This is very important legislation. I wish Conservative Members of Parliament would get up on their feet and talk about it. It is the kind of legislation that previous Conservative Prime Ministers would never have thought of introducing. There is no way the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), if he were still Leader of the Conservative Party, would introduce legislation to privatize one of the most successful Crown corporations in this country, particularly when, once it is privatized, it will become a merchant of death exporting weapons around the world. There is no way under the sun that the Right Hon. Member would ever do that. There is no way that John Diefenbaker would have done that.
What we have now is a new Republican Party. Sort of the Republican Party North. What Ronald Reagan says in Washington, Brian Mulroney will do in Ottawa. This Bill is testimony to that fact. I know that a lot of Members of the Conservative Party are very upset about it. That is why we see a nosedive in the polls like we have never seen before for any Government in the history of Canada. Never before have we seen a party fall, over about eight or nine months, from 60 per cent to 36 per cent. It is a free fall.

It is a free fall, Mr. Speaker.

We have never seen that in the history of Canada, federally or provincially. We have never, never seen a party fall so quickly from public favour. With this kind of legislation that free fall is probably only half finished. Come the next election campaign there will be very few Members of the conservative Party left when Canadians mark their ballots.

Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Cote).

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about the question asked by Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom): Why sell Canadian Arsenals ... Why in his brilliant speech that lasted nearly twenty minutes, did we get all this rhetoric about the sale of Canadian Arsenals? For twenty minutes he trotted out all kinds of frightening, ridiculous and idiotic scenarios, something at which the Socialists are experts. Why, after 40 years, sell a company the Canadian Government no longer needs?
Forty years ago, in 1945, the situation was different. Munitions for defence had to be purchased on the market. Now, 40 years later, the situation has changed.
The Canadian Government is role is to administer the affairs of Canadians and not to operate commercial enterprises. We are not a capitalist institution but a Government institution that administers the business of this country.
The Hon. Member said earlier that the present Government of Ontario also consists of both Socialists and Liberals, who recently sold the Inter Urban Transport Company, also a profitable enterprise, to Lavalin.
However, ten years ago in Toronto they had a problem. The city of Toronto needed interurban transportation equipment. In ten years they developed a technology and built up profitable enterprise that today can be used not just by the city of Toronto but by all of Canada and perhaps all of North America.
Now that is what sensible Governments try to do, while the Socialists, supported by the Liberals, continue to spout their rhetoric and try to interfere, whenever a Government makes a sensible decision. Yes, it is a sensible decision to sell Canadian Arsenals to the private sector because it will help to diversify and create more companies. The raison d'etre of any enterprise should be, first of all, to make a profit, and to make a profit, one must increase sales, produce more, diversify and be competitive.
That is what private enterprise will do with Canadian Arsenals Limited. It will certainly not use it to produce food.
Mr. Speaker, I am amazed anyone would have Canadians believe that the company that purchased Canadian Arsenals Limited will peddle munitions and arms, emphasizing the situation in Nicaragua and elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville why he rose in the House to play the demagogue on such an important Bill, unless he is doing it for the sale of publicity. All he can think of at the present time is the opinion polls. I wonder if he has any other valid reasons, and whether these
Canadian Arsenals Limited
include the interests of middle-income Canadians or, as he keeps saying: "Ordinary Canadians, ordinary Canadians".
Mr. Speaker, for the Conservative Party there is only one kind of Canadian, the real Canadians. As I said the other day, the "extraordinary Canadians" are on the other side of the House. They are the socialists. There are not many of them, and there are very few Canadians in this country who listen to what they have to say.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member from Quebec asked me a question: Why sell the company-

First of all, the company has been quite profitable and made a lot of money in this country, and that is why I want to keep it for the people of Canada and for the Government of Canada. That is one good reason for us to keep the company.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party is now in the process of changing a Conservative tradition and a Canadian tradition. Up until now, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party and the Government of Canada under any Prime Minister- Pearson, Trudeau, Diefenbaker or Clark-have followed the same policy and, traditionally, making munitions has never been geared to profits. It is a very important principle and the present Government is about to change it. Until now we have decided to keep the industry in the public sector because it happens to be a sector where profits are not required, Mr. Speaker, and it has been a Progressive Conservative Party's tradition.
Third, Mr. Speaker, is the significance of public enterprise. The Hon. Member said we are socialists, that we want everything to be state-controlled, and so forth. Well, Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that the Progressive Conservative Party has always been a staunch defender of public enterprise. I vividly recall the policy of John Diefenbaker, and before him came Sir John Macdonald. The Progressive Conservative Party has always been a strong advocate of public enterprise, a time-honoured legagy, Mr. Speaker.
It was the Progressive Conservative Party that set up Radio-Canada, the CBC, not the Liberal Party. It was also the Progressive Conservative Party that established the Canadian Wheat Board, which is another major public enterprise in this country. We owe it to the Progressive Conservative Party. It was also the Progressive Conservative Party that created the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Speaker, not the Liberal Party.

March 11, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
The great Conservative tradition concerning public enterprise exists as well at the provincial level. Two Alberta Conservative Members sit in front of me, and they know that Mr. Lougheed nationalized a number of companies in their province. I remember very well the case of PWA, Mr. Lougheed's airline. He nationalized it, along with many other Alberta companies. The Conservative tradition in Alberta is to have a lot of state-controlled enterprises. Perhaps Mr. Lougheed is a Red Tory, but still it is a major Conservative tradition.
It was the same thing under Mr. Davis in Ontario. It was Mr. Davis and his Progressive Conservative Party who nationalized Suncor, a major oil company. I would suggest that the neophyte Conservative Member from Quebec has no understanding at all of his Party's tradition and roots. The Party of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is not at all the same as Mr. Diefenbaker's Party, Mr. Speaker. This Party has changed its views and policies, it is not the same political Party. As I said in English, we now have the Republican Party of the North. It is a Party like Mr. Reagan's Republican Party, or a Conservative Party like Mrs. Tatcher's Conservative Party in England. It is not the same political Party.
That explains the current drastic drop in the popularity of the Progressive Conservative Party throughout Canada. It is the Party of corporate power, the Party of wealthy people, not the Party of ordinary Canadian men and women.

That is the second mistake the Government is making while trying to sell this corporation. Finally, a study of this corporation was carried out by Mr. Andersen. subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mclnnes that Bill C-87, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-87, an Act to provide for the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited. We are talking about a Crown corporation which is 100 per cent owned by the federal Government. It was formed in 1945 to ease the transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy. Ninety per cent of its sales are to the

March 11, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
federal Government through the Department of National Defence. Canadian Arsenals Limited makes medium and large-calibre ammunition. It had profits of some $11.3 million last year. Yet this company is being offered for sale for some $92.2 million.
We in this Party are asking what reason the Government is giving for this sale. We are not able to perceive any reason except an ideological reason. There is a blind adherence to an ideology that all Crown corporations are somehow wrong. If there is one thing that Conservatives dislike more than Crown corporations that lose money, it is Crown corporations that make money. Here we are talking about a Crown corporation that makes money. Last year the Financial Post ranked Canadian Arsenals Limited as number three in Canada in terms of its five-year profit growth. It is a profitable company with which we are dealing; yet the company is going to be sold by the present Government for some $92.2 million.
I would like to point out to Hon. Members that the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited is not the only example of the Government being led blindly down the privatization path by its adherence to an ideology that has no real connection with the reality of the Canadian economy. The privatization program is not one that is helping the different regions of Canada. I am sure this is true for the region affected by the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited. Certainly it is true on Vancouver Island. There is the proposed privatization both of the Esquimalt drydock and of Teleglobe which has facilities on Vancouver Island.
I would like to illustrate what I mean by dealing with some of the factors involved in the privatization of the drydock at Esquimalt. That facility has a replacement value of some $56.3 million, and since 1978 the federal Government has invested some $30 million in the Esquimalt drydock to make sure that it is an up-to-date, modern facility able to handle virtually any ship on the Pacific coast. It is in fact one of the largest drydocks on the entire Pacific coast, both in Canada and the United States. It is an important facility and an important part of the greater Victoria economy.
The Government's plan for privatizing the drydock has three steps. First the Government will attempt to sell it to a Canadian company. If that is not successful, it will put it out for international tender, and if that is not successful it will then be sold for scrap. What studies have been made about the importance of this facility to the over-all economy of Victoria?
I would like to remind Hon. Members opposite that according to the unemployment statistics that came down last week, Victoria has the highest unemployment rate of any major metropolitan centre in Canada. In fact, the unemployment rate is 16.1 per cent. For Vancouver Island as a whole the unemployment rate is 16.2 per cent.
I would like to know what studies have been done with regard to the impact privatization will have on unemployment. Since the Conservative Government was elected in September 1984, the City of greater Victoria has lost 10,000 jobs. Yet the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Crofton) are Conservative Members. Their ridings have lost 10,000 jobs and we are concerned about that. I expect privatization will make the situation even worse.
We have not seen any attempt by the Government to make the drydock in Esquimalt pay its way. The current rates for work being done in the drydock are badly out of date. They were set in 1971 and they have not been raised since that time. It is no wonder the drydock is losing money. We can presume that any buyer that attempts to operate that drydock will raise the rates.
We can look at the philosophy of privatization as it affects Teleglobe which has a facility at Lake Cowichan in my riding, a facility that employs 19 people. This is another corporation that is making money, just like Canadian Arsenals Limited. The employees of Teleglobe have the same basic concerns as the employees of Canadian Arsenals. They are concerned about job security and their pension rights. They have no guarantee as to what will happen to them. They have not been involved in any kind of meaningful discussion one way or another. The same kind of situation is being faced by the employees of Teleglobe as is being faced by the employees of Canadian Arsenals Limited.
It seems that the policy of privatization being followed by the Conservative Government is almost exactly the same as the policy of privatization that was followed by the Bennett Government in British Columbia, a policy that has resulted in disastrously high unemployment rates and a disastrous economy in general. It is a policy that is tied in with the attempt to starve our economy to health in the belief that if we cut back enough somehow the economy will start blooming and blossoming. That has not worked. There is no recognition of the Government's basic responsibility for the health of the economy. There is no recognition that the Government can be on the side of the people to help provide better lives for them. Instead, there is just a blind adherence to an ideology of privatizing any Crown corporations that exist.
Canadian Arsenals Limited as a Crown corporation selling to the Department of National Defence saves taxpayers money. It helps keep our deficit down. I would like to ask government Members what studies they have done indicating that privatization of Canadian Arsenals Limited will in any way serve the public interest. Is it going to serve the public interest by reducing the cost to the Government for munitions? Is it going to serve the public interest by creating job guarantees? How is the privatization of Canadian Arsenals Limited going to serve the public interest in any way? It will serve the private interest of SNC, the purchaser.
It is interesting to note that SNC gave $1,000 to the campaign fund of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and $10,000 to the 1984 Tory campaign fund. It is very solidly in support of the conservative Party, and the Conservative Party likes to look after its friends in situations such as this. However, I suggest that the Conservative Party and the Conservative Government have a responsibility
March 11, 1986

to Canadian people. We have not seen anything in connection with Canadian Arsenals Limited which suggests that they have even conducted basic studies as to the value to Canadians of privatization. The SNC group operates world-wide, but mainly in Canada and the developing world. Since it is the group which owns the company that provides small calibre ammunition to the federal Government, we are concerned that it will have a monopoly on munitions sales in Canada. We are also concerned about what will happen in terms of munition sales in other parts of the world, particularly in the Third World.
It is interesting to note that in the press release of December 2, 1985, the Minister said that the Government was confident that once the company was privatized, CAL would pursue additional markets and product diversification. Also he indicated that through the sale the Canadian ammunition industry should become internationally competitive, making possible increased sales to our NATO partners. We are concerned that it will not only make possible increased sales to NATO members but indeed, increased sales to Third World countries which should not be putting money into munitions; for that matter, neither should NATO countries. Certainly we are concerned about the idea of a Canadian company becoming involved in the merchandizing of death through armaments.
Also it is interesting that IVI, the only manufacturer of small calibre ammunition in Canada, a subsidiary of SNC, has been found to be supplying arms to the Contras, the rebels in Nicaragua, which follows the whole philosophy of Ronald Reagan trying to destabilize the situation. We have received appeals from all countries in Central America and in South America that there must be a withdrawal of interest by other countries so that the people of Central America can solve their own problems. Here we have a Canadian company selling arms to the Contras, making a handsome profit and trying to destabilize the entire situation. We do not want to see this continual merchandizing of death. We are concerned that it is something that will happen as a result of the privatization of CAL and the sale to the SNC group.
Our Party has some basic concerns about the rights of employees and how they will be affected by the sale. It is interesting that in the same press release of December 2 the Minister indicated that the interests of CAL employees were of paramount importance to the Government in conducting the sale. In particular, SNC must as a condition of the sale, sign a reciprocal transfer agreement to ensure the portability of the pension rights of CAL employees. In addition SNC has agreed to observe the terms of the collective agreement recently ratified by CAL employees.
The interests of CAL employees have not been taken into account in any kind of adequate way by this agreement. They were not consulted prior to the sale being drawn up. They have been unable to look at the agreements to see whether the promises in the press release were present in the agreement. There is no satisfactory agreement with the employees on their pension rights; for example, the question of indexation for
Canadian Arsenals Limited
which they, along with other federal public servants, have paid to guarantee indexation. There has been no agreement on the indexing provision. No information has been made available to the employees as to whether the early retirement provision of their pension plan will still be in effect after the sale. The present plan allows for early retirement at age 55 years, but they do not know what is happening to it. They do not know what is happening to their job security. As I said earlier, there was no consultation prior to the sale.
Since there is a lack of participation on the part of Conservative Members in this debate, we have come to the conclusion that there is no reason for the sale except ideology. It is not in the public interest to proceed with the sale. It is very definitely not in the interests of those employees who are presently working for Canadian Arsenals Limited.
The whole question of private profit should be taken away from the manufacture of munitions rather than putting it back in. Basically that is what the Government is doing by privatizing Canadian Arsenals Limited and by making it available to the SNC group so that it can make a handsome profit. If we are to live in a world where there are conditions of national security which have to be met, let us make sure that we meet those conditions on the best terms possible for all concerned rather than make national security some kind of financial bonanza for one more corporation.
Reference was made this morning and this afternoon to the warning of the late President Eisenhower about the military industrial complex. By privatizing Canadian Arsenals Limited we are encouraging the development of a military industrial complex in Canada. I do not think it is something that should be encouraged. When we look at the whole question of privatization, perhaps there should be a simple test which the Government could apply; that is, that unless there is adequate reason for privatizing it should be left in the public domain. The reverse of that is also true. There should not simply be nationalization for purely ideological reasons. There should be sound reasons on both sides of the debate. If industries are to be nationalized, brought into the public domain, it should be done for very concrete reasons. By the same token, if Crown corporations are to be privatized, it should be done for some very basic, empirical, pragmatic reasons. We do not see those empirical, pragmatic reasons in this particular situation. Instead we see a blind adherence to an ideology that Crown corporations have little or no place in the fabric of Canadian life.
From my own vantage point as a Member from Vancouver Island, I say that privatization will have an adverse impact upon the economy of that region. I am concerned that it will also have an adverse effect on the people of Quebec, the province in which Canadian Arsenals Limited operates. There seems to be a policy on the part of the Government of raising taxes, taking more and more money from individual taxpayers. This means that moneys are taken out of local communities, such as those on Vancouver Island, to be used for whatever purpose by the Government here in Ottawa. However we are not receiving programs which feed money back into the local

March 11, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
economies. In fact, quite the reverse. We are drawing money away from the local economy which will have a strangling effect on it. We have seen nothing in the way of job creation. We have seen the loss of some $16,000 jobs on Vancouver Island since September 1984 when the Government was first elected.
Along with this policy of raising taxes and doing nothing about job creation in areas where it is most needed we have a policy of privatization, of selling off our resources and not letting the Canadian people or the House of Commons know what is involved, of keeping employees in the dark about conditions under which their jobs are being sold out from under them. Privatization is being kept very private. It should be a matter of public information.
Finally there should be tighter controls on the production of munitions in Canada. We do not want to see this simply proliferate in a way that will allow all kinds of private corporations to get involved, not only in producing munitions and selling them at a profit to the Canadian Government, but producing munitions and selling them to Third World countries. If we have legitimate reasons for national security, then it makes sense for us to keep control of the production of our own munitions. It should be done only for purposes of national security, not for purposes of profit.
On this basis, I would like to oppose this Bill. I urge all Members to think very carefully before they rise in support of it.

Government has also failed to understand the very real plight of a lost generation of youth.
