Mr. Speaker, I wish to express amazement at a remark made in the House by the Official Opposition with respect to census commissioners. Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals accused us of political patronage in the selection of census commissioners. Opposition Members have a short memory. Since 1963 the Liberals have had the last word on the appointment of census commissioners, over 20 years to build up their system and dictate their political preferences. I wonder whether they are so lily-white. Before any kind of examination, the official responsible for selecting the commissioners in my riding made it quite clear to our representative that appointments would be made among those who had experience in the 1981 census. For the opposition, one has to be a Liberal to make the grade. Mr. Speaker, I have to say that my commissioners in Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup are just as intelligent if not more, than Liberal applicants.

Mr. Speaker, this year marks the Diamond Jubilee of the Royal Canadian Legion. It was on a rather bleak day in 1926 when Sir Percy Lake, President of the Legion, told the delegates gathered in Vancouver that the future for those who served in the Great War was very difficult indeed. Their first proposal for pensions was practically ignored. The membership was then 11,000. Today this organization, founded on the principles of remembrance, just rights, loyalty and comradeship, has over 1,800 branches. Membership now totals 600,000 people, roughly the size of Winnipeg.
I am certain that Members of this House would like to pay tribute to this great organization as it celebrates 60 years of service to Canada and Canadians, service which has continued in times of peace and war.

Thanks to the Conservative Government, Mr. Speaker, we have two classes of citizens: those who have home mail delivery and those who have not. In the riding of Saint-Leonard-Anjou some families do not have home delivery, yet others, practically next door neighbours, do. Until yesterday we Canadians were proud of the fact that this Government service was universal, but the situation has changed since the advent of the Conservatives. Why should somebody who buys a new house not be entitled to home mail delivery, whereas somebody else who bought a house two years ago does have that right? It is unfair, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Multiculturalism Minister's failure to follow the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) lead on Japanese-Canadian redress, weekly becomes more outrageous and tragic. The Minister does not recognize that the Canadian Government in 19421943 uprooted and dispossessed people who had not been charged with any seditious activity and whose only offence was their Japanese origin. The Minister does not appreciate that there has never been proper compensation for these property losses.
The Minister refuses to negotiate a proper redress and speaks recklessly of the millions that he thinks it might cost. Mr. Speaker, the Minister's skirmishing against the Japanese-Canadian community is repugnant to Canadians. Other Canadians, such as those of Ukrainian origin who came to Canada before 1914 from Austro-Hungary, suffered unjustified internment during wartime.
But these communities recognize that dispossession of the Japanese-Canadian community is a unique precedent the Parliament of Canada must cancel.
Only a properly negotiated redress can do that.

Mr. Speaker, the tabling this morning of the reports of the Task Force on Program Review chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) is of a significance which cannot be overstated.
It is part of the process of reforming the public administration of Canada which got out of control over years of mismanagement and because of the practice of setting up a plethora of programs to deal with every real or imagined problem.
The options outlined in the report will provide the Cabinet with sensible alternatives so the Government can in future be conducted in an efficient, humane, and cost-effective manner which Canada deserves. The thanks of this House and the nation are due to the many Canadians who served so ably on the Task Force on Program Review.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Longueuil riding has a major industrial vocation and is at the heart of Canada's aerospace industry.
Among the corporations in my riding which are directly involved in this industry, there is the Pratt & Whitney corporation which employs over 7,500 workers. The Pratt & Whitney corporation manufactures airplane motors and exports 85 per cent of its production. It contributes very significantly to the economic development of our country.
Our Government recognized recently the importance of the aerospace industry in Canada and the impact it has on our economy by creating 1,000 new jobs in the fine riding of Longueuil.
Mr. Speaker, it is thanks to the kind co-operation which I obtained from the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) that this project has become a reality.

Mr. Speaker, it is incredible to think that, in a nation based on the solid foundation of equality, the federal Government chooses to discriminate against segments of its own work force. I am referring to the system of pay zones designed more than 20 years ago to determine the salaries of selected public servants. The idea was to pay public servants salaries reflective of the regions in which they worked.
There are over 14,000 members of the Union of National Defence Employees who are subject to this form of economic discrimination. There are tens of thousands of other employees in Public Works, Agriculture, Transport, Environment, and other Departments, in similar circumstances. If the Government of Canada can establish universal pay scales for the RCMP, the Armed Forces, Canada Post and, yes, Members of Parliament, no matter what region we may represent, then these dedicated Public Servants deserve no less.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REUNIFICATION OF BULGARIAN FAMILY
speechtext:
Today I want to bring to the attention of the House another case of children trapped behind the Iron Curtain. Ziya Ismailoff, who works in my riding, and his wife, came to Canada from Bulgaria in 1984 to escape religious and political persecution. Their sons, nine and 11 years of age respectively, are being held as "deposits" to ensure the parents return. Bulgarian law prohibits removing children from the country.
Recently one of the Ismailoff children sent his parents a paper airplane with a message, "I want to fly to Canada. I want to fly to you".
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to do everything in his power to see that the Ismailoff family, and the many others like them, are reunited here in Canada.

subsubtopic: BALTIC COMMUNITY'S OPPOSITION TO HIGHWAY TO HEAVEN TELEVISION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representatives of Canada's Baltic community have expressed grave concern over the scheduled March 12 airing of the one-hour program Highway to Heaven on CTV. Rightfully so. The episode depicts a fictitious family named "Baltic" as neo-Nazis terrorizing a concentration camp survivor.
This depiction on national television of a neo-Nazi, who carries as his surname the name of an ethnic group, can only bring lasting damage to the promotion of racial tolerance and sensititivy. It is absolutely contrary to the multicultural fabric of Canadian society to allow such indirect bias, wherein an entire group of citizens is, by implication, maligned.
I therefore join with other concerned citizens and call upon the CTV at the very least either to delete or dub over this offensive reference. The possible defamation of 100,000 Canadians who take pride in their Baltic heritage can and must be averted.
March 11, 1986

subsubtopic: OFFER OF JOB COUNSELLING AND RETRAINING TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Rural Transition Program announced in last month's Budget is a bleak indication of the government's farming philosophy.
The Government wants to help farmers get off the land. It is issuing the golden handshake to the small independent farmers by offering them job counselling and retraining. I will not deny that Canadian farmers are facing a serious financial crisis, but training them to be computer programmers or pipe fitters does not solve the problem. The country needs an innovative strategy designed to foster growth and prosperity on the family farm. Family farms are the backbone of many rural communities. Those people have spent their lives working the land to produce cheap food for Canadians. What are they being offered in return? Encouragement to close the farm gate!
Farmers do not want job counselling and retraining. They need a bold, aggressive approach to keep them on the farm. The Government must meet this current crisis head on. It must not take the easy way out and turn its back on Canadian farmers.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, March 7, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-99, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Given a chance to find my notes, Mr. Speaker, I certainly will take this opportunity to comment on this very important piece of legislation.
Bill C-99, an Act to provide borrowing authority, seeks parliamentary approval for the expenditure of some $22 billion. As I read here, I think that is what it is, twenty-two billion six hundred million dollars, as may be required for public works and general purposes.
Mr. Speaker, since we all know that the Government borrows money, perhaps it might be useful now and then to ask why the Government wants to borrow $22.6 billion. It is a rather impressive and astronomical amount, as my colleague would say. But what we have to understand is that $22.6 billion is the same as 22,600 million dollars. That is a lot of money!
I would like to comment on such borrowing authority in light of the credibility of the Government's projections pertaining to interest rates, oil prices, investments, and the interest costs of those loans, for I think it is imperative to discuss this in the House since it is a public question, a question of interests to be paid by all Canadians. I would like to talk about the debt structure and, finally, the interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, after tabling his Budget on February 26, 1986 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced a Bill asking the House for authority to borrow, as I just said, an amount not exceeding $22.6 billion for the fiscal year 1986-87, namely the fiscal year beginning next April 1 and ending March 31, 1987. That is the fiscal year of the Government. This amount
March 11, 1986

represents the financial requirements of the Government, meaning that exchange operations are excluded, as provided in the 1986-87 fiscal plan. What we have to keep in mind is that it is based on the new accounting practices now in use. Indeed as of this year the Auditor General asked that the accounting methods be changed-and I acknowledge this may be beneficial-and in its Budget the Government has adopted such new accounting methods.
As it happens, Mr. Speaker, I think that the first question has to do with the credibility of the Government's premises because, in our judgment, the premises on which the Government estimates are based have no credibility.
The information now available makes it seem like a real possibility that the deficit will be much higher than forecast. We question for instance the projections related to interest rates, oil prices and investments.
Let us speak first about the interest rates. For 1986, the Government foresees an average interest rate of 9.5 per cent for 90-day bills. However, as we all know, the interest rate was 11.4 per cent as of yesterday, March 10. I do not have today's rate because it is impossible to be always up to date, but yesterday, the rate was at 11.4 per cent, and according to the figures of the Government, every 1 per cent of difference in the interest rate means a difference of about $1 billion in the deficit. I repeat that each upward or downward variation of 1 per cent has a $ 1 billion impact on the deficit. In other words, if the average interest rate for the entire year were 10.5 per cent, for instance, the deficit would be $1 billion over the deficit forecast by the Government. The Conference Board, which is not-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: A two-bit organization?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is not just a two-bit organization, but while it does not refuse to examine minor problems, it is concerned mostly with problems which affect the Canadian economy, and for 1986, this organization has forecast interest rates of 10.4 per cent, that is 1 per cent higher than what the Minister forecast. If we look at the projections of experts like those at the Conference Board, we immediately see that the Government will miss the mark in its projections and will probably take a bad fall as concerns the deficit by exceeding by $1 billion the amount forecast.
Let us now talk about the oil prices. The Government forecasts average oil prices of $22.50 U.S. a barrel until the end of 1986. The spot price, which is the price of oil on the European spot market where oil is sold, is about $12 U.S., or approximately $10.50 under the figure announced in the Budget.

speechtext: Another mistake.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Economic Council of Canada-this is another serious organization, an economic advisory
Borrowing Authority Act
council to the Government-used an average price of $19 U.S. for its economic forecasts. The Conference Board, on the other hand, used a price of $18 U.S. for the second half of 1986, and $21 U.S. for the last part of 1987. Now, for each reduction of one dollar in the price of oil from the estimated price, there is a loss to the Federal Government of $110 million in corporate income tax and gasoline and oil taxes. We can therefore see here net losses, because the forecasts as stated by the Minister of Finance are not accurate. He is wrong in our view on interest rates, and he is wrong on the price of gas and oil.
He stated in his Budget speech that these were the best figures available when the Budget was sent to print.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They did not look very far.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
We told him, Mr. Speaker: If that is true, it is up to you to give new figures, to feed new data into your computer and print out more accurate figures, rather than carrying on with that false theory based on a totally inaccurate assumption.
As far as investments are concerned, the Minister of Finance did forecast in his Budget a growth rate of about 7 per cent for investments in 1986. The most recent survey made by Statistics Canada concerning business investment intentions shows that Canadian business think they will be investing only 2.5 per cent more this year than last. And God knows how important business investment intentions are!
Furthermore, the Minister of Finance estimates that investments in new plants and equipment will be 6 per cent, while Statistics Canada forecasts a 1.9 per cent decline in actual figures, when price increases are taken into account. If Statistics Canada's forecasts were to prove right, the economic growth rate would be lower than the one predicted by the Minister of Finance. And for each reduction of one percentage point in actual economic growth, the deficit once more increases by $1 billion. An error of one per cent in investments expands into a $1 billion increase in the deficit. They were wrong in interest, so an extra $1 billion can be added easily. They were wrong on the price of oil, and there again it is $110 million for each dollar reduction in that price. And we also note, on investment projections, quite a serious error that is supported by agencies as important as Statistics Canada and the Conference Board. So we have here an extra $1 billion increase in the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, this means it is vital for us that the Government review its figures, that it put all the economics back into its computer in order to give Canadians the real answer and the hard facts, which is that those computations are wrong and the data are totally inaccurate.
Let us now look at interest charges, Mr. Speaker, because there is always a cost for money that is borrowed. Interest is like a rent on money, we pay money to someone when that person lends us funds, in the way of interest, or to make it

March 11, 1986
Borrowing Authority Act
simpler as a price for money. It is rather difficult admittedly to figure out interest payments on Government borrowings. This is based of course on the rate of interest charged, on the term of the loan and on the currency in which that debt is designated. This is quite important. Those are the figures which the economists are constantly throwing at us and we are told with great fanfare every Thursday, I believe, what the Bank of Canada interest rate will be during the week. The banks look at it and say: "Well this is good or not so good. We will set the prime rate according to that rate". Then it is increased or reduced. I admit that it is difficult to judge. It is like the Canadian dollar, it depends on the mood of those who have the power to set the bank interest rate and the Canadian dollar rate the following morning.
Mr. Speaker, it is expected that on average the Government will pay 10 per cent. I feel that 10 per cent is a rather realistic average rate on a $22.6 billion loan so that we will only pay interest on that amount for 1986. It is a rather huge sum we have to pay for borrowing money.
Mr. Speaker, such an estimate seems to be rather accurate since the Government says that in 1984-85 on a net debt of $199 billion, they paid in interest alone something like $18 billion or 9.05 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian debt is made up of a large number of items with a great variety of maturities and other characteristics. However, it is possible to break down that debt into a Canadian dollar component and a foreign currency component.
Mr. Speaker, I have in front of me a table showing that on December 31, 1985, 5.2 per cent of the Canadian Government debt was in the form of foreign currencies.

But where has this Member from Winnipeg-Assiniboine been? 1 know he represents the most affluent part of the City of Winnipeg. Surely he cannot be so blind as to imply, as he did in those remarks, that anybody who wants a job can find a job. That is just not true and he should have known that. I think it was the same day he made those remarks that the CBC's The Journal devoted 35 minutes or more of its program to what is happening in British Columbia. There you see the new reality: a Social Credit Government which is concerned only about restraint and keeping the deficit down. The Journal told us that in addition to the fact that one in six people in British Columbia are living below the poverty line, there is a new class which includes 4,000 unemployed teachers and 16,000 persons with university degrees who cannot find jobs. 1 ask Members on the Government side to do some simple arithmetic. How much money did it cost the people of Canada to educate those people? Surely we and they would be much better off if they were working and paying taxes and not drawing unemployment insurance or welfare. Surely it is a tragic failure for this country when these trained people cannot find jobs and use their skills. Some of these people have used up their unemployment insurance benefits and their savings and are now drawing welfare. Some of these people were interviewed while getting food baskets from food banks established by charitable organizations. What a commentary on this country! That is the reality in British Columbia. That province was the first to implement a program of restraint, but the situation is now much worse there than it was in 1981. The unemployment rate then in B.C. was 6.7 per cent and now it is almost twice that level.
Five or six weeks ago I was in Saint John, New Brunswick and Halifax, Nova Scotia. I visited one of those agencies in each city which has been established to help those in need by people who care. I urge all Members of Parliament, regardless of Party, to visit these places. There is one in almost every city in Canada. I visited Romero House in Saint John, New Brunswick. When it started four years ago it was serving 20 to 30 people a day. Now it is serving a hot meal to 200 people a day, seven days a week. It hands out food baskets and is making plans to establish three other places in other parts of the city who will be doing the same thing. Romero House was organized by a very concerned and caring woman, namely, Mrs. Carol McNulty. She is supported by individuals, service clubs and church groups. Some farmers give produce and some stores give the goods they have been unable to sell. It costs about $3,000 a month to operate. The group gets no money from government sources. What interested me was that they do not want money from government sources. They are doing
what they are doing because the need is there. They believe it is a disgrace that in a country as wealthy as Canada hundreds and thousands of people have to depend on charity.
The next day I went to Halifax and visited Hope Cottage. It was started in 1970 by a Catholic priest. It is now feeding 300 people a day. I was told that in the beginning it served older people, 55 and over, and street people. Now, 60 per cent of the people who come there are under 35. A large number are in the age bracket of 16 to 19. Many come from small towns. They have little education, they sleep and eat wherever they can. We have had news reports about people in many cities who have no place to sleep except in an alley or under bridges. We all know what that means in Canada in the winter. Hope Cottage provides meals, a place to stay, and clothing. They counsel people and are trying to make the public and Government aware of the seriousness of the problem.
I also visited Adsum House, which is very close to Hope Cottage, where they try to help homeless women, and the North End Community Clinic which is trying to organize improvements in the health services for poor people. These are the realities which this Budget and this borrowing Bill completely ignore.
I talked about British Columbia and the three years during which that province followed the kind of restraint program which this Government is imposing on the people of Canada. Surely we can learn a lesson from British Columbia. The idea of restraint which the Conservative Members of this Parliament are proposing is exactly the same kind of idea which was proposed and implemented in British Columbia. It did not work there and it is not going to succeed here. This is why it did not work.
Public sector lay-offs, and that is what we are getting here, and wage restraints, did not give the consumer in British Columbia any confidence in the Government so as to spend money and increase demand. Those Government employees who lost their jobs were not absorbed into the private sector labour force. This obviously did not reflect investor confidence in these measures. The Government did not save money by laying people off. In fact, it had to pay out money in the form of welfare and other benefits. The British Columbia Government's ideological agenda blocked any significant recovery of the economy at a time when the rest of Canada was starting to emerge from the recession of 1981-83. Wages were capped, cutting demand, massive unemployment was accepted by that Government, and it is going to be accepted by this Government. Low paid and unorganized labour was encouraged to grow at the expense of higher paid workers, and education and social services were cut back. That is precisely what this Conservative Government is proposing. This Government is proposing to bring the B.C. model to Canada as a whole. It was wrong in British Columbia and it is going to be just as wrong in the rest of the country. It is for those reasons that we oppose this borrowing Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have here in my hand Bill C-99, an Act to provide borrowing authority, which we are debating at this time. It is
March 11, 1986

interesting that in three short paragraphs, on one single page, this Government is asking for permission to borrow $22.6 billion. Why? To carry out, we are told, the policies of this Government which have been put forward over the last year and a half. As I consider this Bill, I have to ask: Do these policies, clearly laid out by two Tory Budgets, two sets of Estimates and an Economic Statement, meet the needs of the people of my riding or, for that matter, the people of Canada as a whole? Do these policies really fulfil the aspirations of our people? I do not think I need to refer to opinion polls to come to my own conclusion and that my answer on behalf of the constituents to whom I speak, is an emphatic no. I am inclined to tell the Government that I do not really wish to see it borrow this money until it shows that it cares more about people and less about statistics, until it is prepared to care more about the average man and less about the wealthy.
The names I am using now are fictitious, of course, but the people and the stories they have are not. Ruth Jones in my riding is a single mother with two children. She is working as a secretary. She wants to take her BA at night school. She applied, but she cannot get in. Apparently we are finding that the universities are not able to take a person like her into evening courses because the seats are taken.
Joe Smith wants to help his son Jim to fulfil his dream to become a computer science graduate. Jim applies, he cannot get in. There are only 40 students who get in while the department receives 700 applications. Ruth Jones, the single mother secretary who wanted to improve her education, finds that her income is stuck, stuck forever with no hope for advancement, she feels. Joe Smith will never become a computer scientist. The university he applied to has no room for him because it does not have the money to fund any more seats in this course. Government cut-backs for post-secondary education have caused the university to be unable to serve people like Joe Smith.
These are real people. This is what the future of postsecondary education in this country is like. These people are illustrative of the impact of the cut-backs by the Tories to post-secondary education. They want to borrow money to fulfil their policies, but their policies are to cut back on post-secondary education. This is the reality of the full cut as a result of Tory incompetence and shortsightedness.
The federal Government has announced and now has brought in Bill C-96, which will change the formula by which transfers of support by this Government for post-secondary education will take place. It is reducing the formula for these transfers by 2 per cent per year. This will result in a cumulative cut to post-secondary education by 1990-1991 of aproxi-mately $2 billion, $2 billion out of an education system that has been trying to fight a war on behalf of the youth of our country who cannot find jobs and have been returning to the post-secondary educational system in droves in the hopes that they can advance their education sufficiently to qualify themselves to get those jobs which they need to have to carve out

for themselves a future. This avenue is now being closed to them as well, no jobs and now no studying.
Faced with increased costs, the unviersities have also faced declining budgets. As David L. Johnson, President of the 79-member Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the AUCC, stated, "No government can make the claim of fiscal responsibility if it puts at risk the very institutions on which Canadians depend for their future.
Post-secondary education is but one example of how this Government's latest Budget is one of doom and despair for the youth of this country. At a time when youth unemployment is running at 15.9 per cent, where are the opportunities for jobs for young people? How can they train adequately for the future when budgets to colleges, CEGEPs and universities are cut; when federally paid for seats for university training programs and colleges are by 40 per cent; when colleges and university employment offices are cut back and closed down; when job-training programs in 1987-1988 will be cut by another $100 million on top of the $200 million cut for 1986-87 unveiled in last May's Budget?

It cuts funds to post-secondary education contrary to the recommendations. It cuts funds for retraining programs, funds for job-creation, it cuts out the First Chance program, it cuts out Katimavik, a youth program whose obvious success is evident in that there have been some 20,000 graduates, a program which at the time it was cut was receiving some 500 applications a week. It was a program which provided services by youth at a salary of $1 a day to the elderly, to the handicapped and to such worth-while projects as reforestation and environmental and community improvement. It is amazing. This is a United Nations prize-winning program. This is program which has been endorsed by the municipalities of Canada. A 20-year-old, for example, on his own and jobless costs Canadian taxpayers from $3,000 to $9,000 for nine months. The person contributes nothing to society. many of our youth do not get full-time jobs and, if they do, many of them are low-paying jobs that have been created by corporations by laying off older employees in order to take advantage of Government programs. It is crushing our young people and their ability to contribute to the economic, cultural and moral growth of Canada. The state of our universities and colleges leaves young people without hope.
I want to deal with the voluntary sector, including the charitable organizations and community organizations. This sector has proven to be one of the largest and most intensive job creation sectors in Canada. It is an intensive labour market

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-99, which would give the Government authority to borrow some $22.6 billion so that it can carry out its program. Our problem with this Bill is that we do not like the Government's program because it fails completely to address the real needs of Canada at the present time. As presented in the Budget two weeks ago what we have is a program which increases taxes, cuts government programs and does absolutely nothing with respect to jobs. It has an emphasis on the deficit, which is misplaced because by its actions in throttling the economy the deficit will not go down as hoped.
I wish to emphasize in the few minutes I have this afternoon the absolute need for jobs and the absolute need for the Government to address this situation. 1 wish to focus my remarks on British Columbia, and Vancouver Island in particular, because I think the situation there stands out in very stark contrast to the situation in the rest of the country.
The situation in British Columbia makes me ask where the 19 Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament were when the Budget was being drawn up. I must also ask where the three members of Cabinet from British Columbia were when it was being prepared. Why is there not something in the Budget which would help to deal with the problems in British Columbia? There is nothing. Since the Conservative Government was elected in 1984 the City of Victoria has lost 10,000 jobs. Some 16,000 jobs have been lost on Vancouver Island. In February, our youth unemployment stood at 22.1 per cent. When we look at the figures for long-term unemployment in British Columbia we see a very desperate situation. Some 65,000 of the unemployed in British Columbia have been unemployed for six months or more. This represents 31.4 per cent of all the unemployed in British Columiba. That is the highest percentage in all of Canada. When we look at the unemployment who have been unemployed for over one year we see the same story. Some 29,000 British Columbians have been unemployed for a year or more. This represents 14.2 per cent of all unemployed British Columbians. Again, this is the highest average in all of Canada, some 40 per cent higher than the national average with respect to people who have been unemployed for longer than one year.
We must combine these statistics, which have to be looked at in terms of real human beings and the suffering which they are experiencing, with the lack of programs introduced by the federal Government. Last year the Government trumpetted a great deal about the federal-provincial forestry agreement. This agreement was to see some $300 million of federal-provincial funds for British Columbia forests over the next five years. However, foresters in that province say that in order to address adequately the situation in British Columbia, which is at a crisis point, there should be at least twice that amount of money. Certainly in terms of employment needs it should be twice that amount of money. However, there is nothing in the Budget to help our forests.
With respect to fisheries, the Minister promised in February that if the users could ante-up with one-third of the money, about $100 million, the federal Government would put in $200 million to establish a $300 million salmonoid enhancement program for the next five years. The fact is that user groups, particularly commercial fishermen, are completely unable to meet the request for $100 million at the present time. Anyone who has followed the situation on the West Coast, and certainly all Members from British Columbia should have done so, knows that British Columbians have gone through a number of very difficult years. There have been poor catches and not great prices, high interest rates and high gas and oil prices. Last year was a good year and British Columbians were just

beginning to catch their breath. The Government is now trying to blackmail them with the idea that there will be a salmonoid enhancement program only if they come up with this $100 million user fee. As one British Columbian said, it is like throwing an anchor to a drowning man. Instead of putting money into British Columbia to help it recover from the recession, what we have seen from the Government in its November, 1984 Economic Statement, last May's Budget and the present Budget, has been a series of unfair taxes loaded on low and middle-income people.
These taxes total some $1,300 for the average family. This money is being taken not only from individuals but from every family. It is being taken away from their communities such as the communities of Duncan, Sooke, Colwood, Chemainus and Ladysmith. This is money which comes to Ottawa for whatever purposes the Government wishes to put it to.
This money is being removed from local communities where it could circulate and do some good toward helping sustain a large and fragile economy. It is being removed from local communities which will have an even more depressing effect on the province. One of the most unsettling facts about this situation is the unfairness of it all. The fact is that wealthy income earners will be paying lower taxes because of the reduction of the surtax at the end of this year while all other Canadians will be hit with a 3 per cent surtax on their income tax.
Since the Conservatives came to power we have seen three increases in the federal sales tax of one percentage point apiece. This directly hits low-income people. In the Budget we saw some help for Atlantic Canada, which I know is not enough. I know that Atlantic Canada has very serious longterm problems. However, Atlantic Canada received more help than did British Columbia. British Columbia received nothing. In considering the situation of women and children we see nothing. The last word the Government had for women and children came when it cut the indexing with respect to family allowances. Instead of moving quickly to address what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognized as a serious situation in the election campaign, that is, the need for adequate and affordable day care for all Canadians coast to coast, the Government has chosen to appoint a parliamentary committee which will tour Canada and hear submissions. Gulf Refinery
Mr. Speaker, this matter goes back to the summer of 1984, and we are still discussing it today. The Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) is wrong when he says it started under the Liberals. He is wrong, Mr. Speaker, and I hope he will listen carefully, because his credibility is at stake.
Mr. Speaker, during the summer of Olympia & York, Petro Canada and the federal Government proceeded with the purchase of the assets of Gulf. Early in September, thanks to the efforts of a number of Conservative members, Olympia & York was persuaded to postpone closing the refinery for two months. I take my hat off to those Members, and they are the Hon. Member for Mercier (Ms. Jacques) first of all, and then to some extent the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) and the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin)!
Mr. Speaker, matters got worse, and today, we have reached the point where the refinery is closed down, 450 employees have lost their jobs, and a Conservative Minister has resigned. A number of Conservative Members have lost all credibility with the public on this matter.
To me, the credibility of Conservative Members is not the main thing. That is their problem, not mine and not that of the people of Canada. What is still at stake today is the credibility of the Prime Minister, and also the interests of Quebec consumers and 450 employees of the Gulf refinery in Montreal East.
I know that those people are watching us, and I hasten to commend the representatives of the Gulf refinery workers for all their work and efforts to save jobs in Montreal East and soften the blow against Quebec consumers.
Mr. Speaker, those workers had confidence in all Members of all political persuasions, at both federal and provincial levels, but they wake up today and they are out of a job. Still, they know who is telling the truth in this matter.
What happened? How is it that we in the Liberal Party, the Official Opposition, are involved in this case which took place in the riding of a Conservative Member, the Member for Mercier?
For starters, it all began after the announced closing of four Montreal East companies, and those people called on us to support them on the picket line. I knew full well that as a plant worker I would never have accepted a politician showing up at the plant gate just to have his picture taken, shake a few hands and drive back home. So I agreed, along with my colleagues- the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) and the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre)-on the condition that we would regroup as the Eastern Townships residents had done, set up a survival committee made up of people from all political parties, and make an honest effort to save as many jobs as possible.
So it was to deal with the Gulf issue, the Canadian Steel Wheel issue, the Vickers issue, the Daoust issue, the Parisette and Bombardier issues that all employee representatives, all elected representatives at the three levels of government, no matter their political stripes, got together under one blanket organization, the Comite de survie de Test de Montreal. And even the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) who is not directly connected with this area attended the first meeting.
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate all provincial candidates, men and women, who took part during their election campaign without ever trying to make political gains.
But newspaper reports will indicate that the three or four Conservative Members included were the only committee members who were in disagreement. It was not a Liberal candidate haggling with the PQ candidate, but the Hon. Member for Montreal-Mercier (Ms. Jacques) who quarrelled with the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) and the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce). The only people who made nuisances of themselves during the Montreal East battle were the three Conservative Members who constantly argued and tried to destroy one another. What happened here in the House? They are the same Conservative Members who brought in Gaz Metropolitan. The Quebec caucus of the Progressive Conservative Party, as its chairperson can bear witness here, supported this initiative. But what happened is that everybody let down the Hon. Member for Terrebonne in this issue.
How did we learn about the sale on December 3, the day after the provincial election? How did we learn about the transaction? What happened at the consumer level? Let us forget for a while about jobs and let us think about the interests of consumers.
On January 18, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post (Mr. Cote), a Quebec Minister of the Crown, a Conservative Minister.. . Ottawa could repudiate the sale of Gulf to Ultramar. This goes against the interests of Quebec consumers. The Minister made the following statement on the 17th, at a press conference which 1 was attending. Shell Canada is threatening to close its refinery in Montreal East and the Quebec National Assembly agrees unanimously to a motion on December 18, if you recall, immediately after the election. To my knowledge, the Liberals and PQ Members are not that friendly. These people unanimously asked that the Canadian Government and the Prime Minister, who prides himself on being the little guy from Baie

Comeau and who has been named citizen for life of West-mount, wait 90 days before agreeing to the transaction.

Member, and I know it is perhaps unusual in the House to say anything good about a Member of another party, but I want to say that we have here a good Member who has worked hard for his constituents in Montreal East. There were also many members from the provincial legislature. One was Louise Harel, a member of the Parti quebecois whom I know very well. She is the provincial member for the riding of Maisonneuve, and she is also very actively involved in the problems of Montreal East.
Mr. Speaker, the issue involving Gulf and Ultramar is a very important one, and it is perhaps one of the reasons why the Conservative party has lost so many points in the polls. I think everybody knows the Conservative Party experienced a free fall in Quebec. According to the SORECOM polls, taken two or three weeks ago, the Liberal Party got 47 per cent of the vote, the Conservative Party 27 per cent and the New Democratic Party, 26 per cent. The Conservative party has nearly become the third party in Quebec.
The poll organizer in Winnipeg said exactly the same thing three or four days ago. He said the NDP now had 25 per cent of the vote in Quebec, the Conservative Party 27 per cent and the Liberal Party, 44 per cent.
One of the reasons for the swift free fall in Quebec, even with 58 Conservative Members from that province in the House, is the fact that the Conservative Party closed down the refinery in Montreal East. This is no joke. This is not a laughing matter. Maybe the Hon. Member from Quebec should go to Montreal East and talk to the workers and talk to the people. Everybody down there knows perfectly well it was the Conservative Party with its decision regarding Investment Canada that closed down the Gulf refinery in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, Ultramar bought the Gulf refinery in Montreal to close it down and get more customers for its refinery in Quebec city. That is the only reason Ultramar purchased the refinery in Montreal East. Otherwise it would not have turned down offers to purchase the Montreal East refinery, by parties such as Gaz Metropolitain, which would have increased competition on the Quebec market.
I know it was a Conservative Member from Montreal East, the Member for Montreal-Mercier (Ms Jacques) who said just before Christmas that Gaz Metropolitain might be a prospective buyer.
However, Mr. Speaker, when the sale of Gulf by Ultramar was examined by Investment Canada, Ultramar threatened to close down its refinery in Quebec City if the Government tried to keep the Gulf refinery open.
Mr. Speaker, it was the pressure of the big multinationals, and unfortunately, the Government listened to the multinationals and not to the people of Quebec.
The same threats were made publicly by Shell Canada which also has a refinery in Montreal. Shell Canada was doing exactly the same thing as Ultramar, the British Corporation, had done.
Mr. Speaker, there is also the matter of undercapacity in Quebec. Now that Gulf has shut down, the Province of Quebec has only three refineries left-Ultramar, Gulf and Petro-Canada. Those companies will now be in a position to boost their refining capacity from 75 to 100 per cent, and their profits will increase accordingly. The companies will also be able to sell all their products to their own retailers, which might signal the demise of independent retailers. That is an important issue because in Quebec as elsewhere in Canada there are quite a few independent retailers whose main problem is to remain competitive, Mr. Speaker.
Everybody, including the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote), the Minister of Energy of Quebec and independent retailers, they all agree that Quebec refining capacity will no longer be able to meet the needs of Quebecers.
At long last the O'Farrell report was finally made public, and it states that Quebec's refining undercapacity will lead to price controls by those three companies-Petro-Canada, Gulf and Ultramar-as well as excessive prices for Quebec consumers. Mr. Speaker, the current situation is such that crude oil prices are tumbling throughout the world. As I recall, a barrel
March 11, 1986

of oil cost $38 three months ago, but according to this morning's Globe and Mail a barrel of oil is selling for only $14 or $15, a drop of $23 or $24 a barrel.
But the main question is this, Mr. Speaker: Why did the Conservative Government give in to the oil industry and ask for the Gulf shutdown? Why did the Government wait for the major company, Ultramar? Secondly, Mr. Speaker, why did the Government not take action to protect the interests of Gulf workers and Quebec consumers? And thirdly, Mr. Speaker, why did the Government imitate the Liberal Party which, a few years ago, closed down three refineries in Montreal? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party and this Government are not the only ones who closed a refinery in Montreal. When Mr. Trudeau was Prime Minister, the Liberal Party closed not one or two but three refineries in that great Canadian city.
Mr. Speaker, the Combine Investigation Bureau should carry out a new inquiry in order to determine whether or not the oil industry is responsible for the Gulf refinery shutdown. Shell and Ultramar together threatened the Government which gave in to pressure.
Mr. Speaker, it is a question of great importance for the Quebec people. It is a question of employment, of "jobs" for many people in Montreal East. It is also an important question on the national level, due to the fact that we now have in the country many, in fact too many foreign businesses, and a lot of foreign control in our economy. This Montreal refinery could be sold to Canadian interests, to a Quebec buyer, such as Gaz Metropolitan. Yet, in spite of the situation, the government and the Minister for Industry have decided to sell this large corporation to a British firm. Mr. Speaker, I know that Quebec people do not agree at all with this decision. I know that because, three or four months ago, I met with many Quebecers, as I said before when I was in the East end of Montreal, with Mrs. Louise Harel, the Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie, and 50 other people.

speechtext:
I am greateful for this opportunity to speak about a subject which we consider very important. As all the Hon. Members are aware, the Federal Government is committed to the creation of a new economic environment in Canada in which, and this is the crucial point, industry and commerce will be able to develop in every region in Canada. One of the troubling facts about a competitive market is that, sometimes, decisions have to be made which will mean plants closing and jobs lost. In such cases, we call upon the Governments to use all available resources to solve the problems.
The Government of Canada has stopped governing the country with ad hoc short term policies. The Progressive Conservative Government is governing the country in a much longer term perspective.
The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Male-part) gave us a history lesson a while ago. I would like to do the same. If we look at what happened in December 1985, Ultramar and Gulf Canada announced that, on January 8, 1986, Ultramar would acquire the capital assets of the refinery and the marketing operations of Gulf Canada located in Quebec and the Atlantic region. It was then decided to close the Gulf refinery in Montreal. Ultramar took over the facilities with the intentions of using them as a terminal for oil products.
The decision to close the Montreal refinery was taken following an evaluation of the refining capacity in Quebec. Closing the Gulf refinery will allow the Ultramar refinery in Quebec City to remain viable.
Mr. Speaker, such are the facts which led to this transaction during 14 months between February 1983 and May 1984. Under the former Liberal Government, nine refineries were closed in Canada, including three in Montreal. This brought about the lay-off of 1,870 employees, including 1,080 in Montreal. As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) pointed out last January 13 when he replied to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and asked him what he did when Esso, BP and Texaco were closed and 1,080 jobs were lost in Montreal East, he should explain his own behaviour then. He did nothing. Where was he when the then

March 11, 1986
Gulf Refinery
Government announced that it was all over for the petrochemical industry and Petromont?
As for us, within a few weeks, we injected $15 million in Petromont and we have just injected $55.8 million in this company to guarantee a viable petrochemical industry in Montreal. That is progress. That is building on solid bases. For about 10 years, oil demand has gone down considerably in Quebec. The market share of natural gas has nearly doubled since 1980, when it was about 8 per cent, as it has now reached 15 per cent. The share of electricity has also increased substantially, from 27 per cent in 1980 to 38 per cent in 1985.1 do not know whether the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) recalls the target set by the Quebec Government in its 1978 energy policy, which was a 41 per cent share of the market for electricity and a 15 to 20 per cent share for gas by 1990. The Government has therefore nearly succeeded in meeting its objective, and it has done so five years before the original target date. That increase in the market share of competing energies resulted in a similar decrease in oil sales, which used to account for more than 70 per cent of energy consumption in Quebec in the early 70's. In 1980, that proportion was reduced to a little over 60 per cent, and, finally, in 1985, oil only accounted for about 45 per cent of energy consumption in Quebec. The unavoidable result of that lower consumption was a refining over-capacity for oil products. Selling the Gulf Corporation facilities is one of the steps in the industry redeployment required because of those structural market changes. The selling of the Gulf assets in Quebec and in the Atlantic area remains a private transaction between buyer and seller, over which the Government has no control. The significant decrease experienced in oil consumption is the major factor in the decision to shut down refineries. The market shift from heavier products to lighter ones and the capital investments required to update plant and equipment also have been contributing factors to the shut-downs which affect all regions in Canada. The reduction in the Quebec production, which at times may seem disproportionate, was caused by the relatively fast decline in demand for oil products. 1 noted that my hon. colleague is concerned about the possibly negative impact of that shut-down on Quebec consumers. I want to reassure this House that Quebec's security with respect to supplies of oil products is not predicated upon its self-sufficiency in the area of refining capacities. I would like to give the House an example. Some provinces like Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba, have no refineries. The State of New York, with 15 million people, has no capacity in that area other than a small asphalt plant. The security of supplies is no major concern in those areas, and this is because they do not feel they need to have refining facilities of their own capable of coping with their internal needs. Quebec market forces in 1985 have been boosted by deregulation, which gave Quebec easier access to products from international sources, at competitive prices. The Hon. Member also referred earlier to the O'Farrell Report, about which he made
a great fuss. As is often the case in his comments, he was looking at only part of the question. And indeed he does that very often in this House. If we had a look at what the report states, and especially what the author wrote, and I quote: This document is not the report of an inquiry under the Act. It was rather a brief of a consultative nature which had been submitted to the Minister.
Such is the O'Farrell Report. It contains not recommendations but assumptions, scenarios based on a market that includes Quebec, Eastern Ontario and the Northwestern United States. The under-capacity to which it referred must be viewed from that angle, as a market that covers part of the North American continent rather than a market limited to the Province of Quebec.
We should certainly not be mixing apples and oranges. I think that is quite clear in fact for anyone who has appraised himself of the contents of that document.
As far as safe supply is concerned, as I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this is what Mr. O'Farrell has to say: "It is an irrelevant question in the context of a competition oriented policy".
I wish Hon. Members would use this report as it was intended to be, and not for the kind of partisan debate that never allows us to take a good look at what is in the files.
Turning to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Speaker, there was a recent survey of the refining capacity and the internal demand in Quebec. That survey concluded that there was an over-capacity in 1985, when Gulf was still operating. Although the Gulf refinery was closed in January 1986, there is still an over-capacity.
That survey was completed, Mr. Speaker, and is presently being studied along with four other studies by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission.
Let us now turn to the investments made by those refineries specifically in Quebec. Some $500 million were invested in the last five years in refining and marketing projects. Other investments amounting now to $215 million will be made in the years to come by Shell and Ultramar. The purpose of such investments is to enlarge the capacity in Quebec and therefore the operating range of the refineries.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind Hon. Members in this House that last fall we asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mrs. Carney) to postpone by two months the closing of the Gulf refinery in order to encourage possible buyers to come forward. That request was accepted and officials from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Departmental of Regional Industrial Expansion gathered the information and analysed the economic projections of offer and demand in order to assist potential bidders needing that information.

Earlier on, my colleague for Montreal-Saint-Marie (Mr. Malepart) mentioned the figures given by some companies. Of course it was in the interest of the Government that potential bidders have access to the basic information in order to be able to bid for Gulf, and to try and co-operate with every effort made by Members of Parliament and Departmental staff to make such bids possible.
Throughout the negotiating process and until the final date, interested parties discussed a possible purchase of the Montreal refinery without reaching a conclusion. However, there is still an interest in buying the petro-chemical facilities within the refinery, and Ultramar will study any commercially feasible proposal. The final date for the submission of bids was even postponed to June 1 1986.
I am sure that if my Hon. colleague had read today's papers, he would at least have learned that that final date for bids was postponed until June 1986.
However, Mr. Speaker, the oil industry in Quebec remains extremely active and the Government spares no effort to support it.
For instance, Petromont received a grant of $55 million from the federal Government in order to upgrade its facilities, and this grant is to be matched by the Quebec government.
Among the other investments made over the last two years in the petrochemical industry in Quebec, Petro-Canada built in Montreal a cracking unit using the new CANMET process. The total cost of this project is $135 million, and it created 30 jobs. I would also like to say that much of the equipment needed for this plant was manufactured by the Vickers Company in Montreal; this is obviously of interest to the workers of Montreal... Petro-Canada is also building a catalytic cracking unit for a total cost of $60 million which will make it possible to keep the present jobs in the Montreal facilities of the company. This unit, just like the CANMET plant, was opened in November 1985.
Shell also announced last December an investment of $80 million in its Montreal facilities in order to replace the catalytic cracking unit and maintain the number of jobs at the present level. Perhaps it is also worth mentioning that the Ultramar Company completed in 1983 its new facilities in Saint-Romuald, near Quebec City, at a cost of $310 million. This investment created some 80 new jobs.
Mr. Speaker, any job loss certainly worries this Government. We are particularly concerned about the future economic situation of the Montreal area. This is why we have formed a Cabinet committee to find ways for this area to continue leading the economic development of Canada, and particularly that of the Province of Quebec.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote Mr. Claude Piche, Executive Commissioner of the Commission d'initiative et des developpements economiques de Montreal who said: "According to the press, the East end of Montreal is an area of
Gulf Refinery
desolation. In fact, the City of Montreal has also successfully contributed to industrial development projects between June 1984 and December 1985. More than 4,000 jobs have been created or maintained in East end Montreal, over a period of just 18 months." And I am still quoting: "Go and ask the 900 employees of MacDonald Tobacco if they are pleased with the $50 million investment at the corner of Iberville and Ontario Streets. Go and ask the employees of Johnson and Johnson if they are pleased with the $32 million investment on Pie IX Boulevard."
Mr. Speaker, through DRIE alone, since September 1, 1984, we have helped create some 17,000 direct jobs in Quebec. Contributions for the Montreal area were close to $279 million. These figures reflect the creation of 8,000 jobs, most of which are in the small business sector.
Mr. Speaker, I wish Opposition Members were not so negative in their comments. They should ask some companies like Balcan Plastics, Cari-All Inc., Industries Genetic and Tye-Sil, what they think of the assistance they received from our Government in East end Montreal. We are going to inject some $10 million to create even more jobs.
Finally, Mr. Speaker... instead of shouting, my hon. colleague might help our Government to create even more jobs for the Montreal area.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-PLACEMENT OF CN MARINE FERRY ORDER. (B) LAUZON SHIPYARD
SHIPBUILDING-PLACEMENT OF CN MARINE FERRY ORDER. (B) LAUZON SHIPYARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say something more about the state of the shipbuilding industry and specifically about the contract from CN Marine for the construction of a second passenger and vehicle ferry to be constructed at a Canadian yard, which subject has been before the House on a number of occasions over the past months. Last Thursday there was a demonstration on this Hill in Ottawa by more than 600 workers from the Versatile Davie Shipyard in Lauzon, Quebec. These workers came to Ottawa in 16 buses and were greeted here by some of the more foul weather this city has produced during the winter. The weather all too sadly reflected the kinds of economic circumstances in which their industry finds itself.
Hundreds of these workers had been at work not many months ago on the construction of the motor vessel Caribou. It is a vessel which represents a most important addition to the fleet of CN Marine. With the vessel now very near completion, and with most of the workers on unemployment insurance, the yard which normally employs 1,600 workers has presently something over 100 employees at work. The workers from Versatile Davie in Lauzon wait in a desperate anxiety for a decision to be made by CN Marine on the purchase of another vessel like the Caribou which they would dearly love to build at their yard on the St. Lawrence.
The nature of my question can be focused if we look at a statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) in November of 1984. In response to a question

March 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
regarding ferry service on the Atlantic coast he said, and I quote from Hansard at page 217:
There will be a rationalization of the Gulf ferry services and the coastal ferry services. As a matter of fact, there will be an additional three new vessels on the Gulf service and one new vessel on the Newfoundland-Labrador coastal service. These vessels will be of the latest state of the art; they will be faster, they will be larger, and they will provide more flexibility and more reliable service. Not only that, this will have a tremendous impact upon the shipbuilding industry and, therefore, will create jobs.
Clearly, the Minister of Transport, who was described by my colleague from Regina this afternoon as an honest and honourable Member of Parliament and Minister, promised something about which so many of us who are concerned about the industry-and pre-eminently, the workers at Versatile Davie in Lauzon-have been looking for, a decision by the Government.
The question has been raised in the House a number of times. I put it to the Minister of Transport on October 29, 1985. At that time I decried the delay which was occurring. The Minister at that time asked: "Should we be dictating to the board?" Well, I think there is reason to dictate to the board. The Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) spoke to this matter a couple of days later last October. The Minister again suggested that they were respecting the board's concerns.
On November 5, 1 spoke on this very same Adjournment Debate and expressed the necessity for the Government to make a decision on this matter. The months passed. I think ruefully of the fact that last June, I pressed the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) on the matter of policy for the shipbuilding industry. I asked him if we were going to have to wait months and months for a decision about an industry which finds itself in circumstances more depressed than those in the 1930s.
The Minister served up: "No, Mr. Speaker". It is going on eight-and-a-half months since then and the Government has done absolutely nothing of a new sort. There have been no new initiatives taken. There may be matters in the wind such as the matter of the Polar 8 ice-breaker, which is still under consideration by the Government in spite of the promise given last September. Yet we continue to wait.
It seems to me that there is a very good case to be made for instructing CN Marine to get on with it and to place the contract. If we have to spend the money on the purchase of a vessel abroad, which appears to be the alternative, that will cost us in terms of foreign exchange. It will bring in some duty to the Government, if they duty is not remitted. However, it will cost us in terms of foreign exchange and place an additional pressure on the dollar. What we have in Canada at Lauzon are workers who are surely costing the better part of $20 million in terms of unemployment insurance on an annual basis. When we consider paying that type of money in unemployment insurance and consider the construction of a vessel which will cost us no more than $120 million or so, it seems to me that we have every reason to get on with it, make a
decision, place the order and put the workers back to the jobs they like so well-construction of vessels on the St. Lawrence.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the concerns of my colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipi-gon (Mr. Epp) regarding a situation that currently prevails in Canadian shipyards. In fact, my hon. colleague has stressed those concerns on several occasions in this House.
I would like to remind him that in a reply he was given by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) on March 6 of this year, the Minister indicated that the Canadian Government was the main purchasing agent for work at shipyards. To help the Hon. Member appreciate what this means, I would like to point out that today, 90 per cent of shipbuilding contracts in our yards are Government contracts. Furthermore, 60 per cent of the work in repair shops is carried out on Government ships. The Canadian Coast Guard's current construction program includes 18 ships, while the total contract is worth over $465.2 million.
Contracts from Ports Canada and CN Marine for the construction of new ships total $143 million.
Transport Canada and a number of Crown corporations may allocate further amounts for other contracts.
As for the new ferry, I think it was said several times in the House that the matter will be submitted to Cabinet within the next few weeks, and so that an answer to the Hon. Member's question may be forthcoming.

subtopic: THE BUDGET-FAMILY INCOME STANDARDS. (B) REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF TAX CREDIT
THE BUDGET-FAMILY INCOME STANDARDS. (B) REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish the previous debate could have finished on a more positive note, but I have the impression that on the Gulf issue, all Conservative Members including the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) were determined to talk the motion out and let all those jobs be lost.
Mr. Speaker, my question concerns an announcement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) regarding prepayment of the child tax credit. In light of a question I had asked the Minister of Finance, I must say in all honesty that perhaps he did not quite hear me, or he misunderstood my question, or again perhaps I did not express myself clearly, but the answer was not good enough.
Mr. Speaker, so as to be sure to get a clear and specific answer, I will repeat my question. It has to do with the prepayment of the child tax credit. The Minister of Finance is patting himself on the back and trying to make us believe that he has helped poor families in that respect. In Canada there are 538,000 people or families who receive the child tax credit. The upper limit set by the Minister of Finance, by the
March 11, 1986

Conservative Government, is $23,500. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker-and this is the question I asked the Minister-he has decided that only those families with a maximum income of $15,000 will be eligible for the $300 child tax credit prepayment, a highly commendable measure which the Liberals and community groups had suggested to the Minister last year. This is not a Conservative invention, they simply cannot come up with constructive measures. But here again, as in the case of the spouse's allowance for the elderly, this Government is wont to discriminate.
What 1 was asking the Minister, and I did not get an answer then, but I trust that someone will give me one now, was why
538,000	Canadian families will not be entitled to the prepayment of the child tax credit according to the statement published by the Minister. There will be a prepayment to prevent people from going to the loan sharks and tax discounters, but in the case of a family with four or five children and an income of $16,000, since it often happens that both spouses work, why did the Government decide that such families will be at the mercy of the tax discounters? If it has a social philosophy, why did the Government not say: Last year, we decided that the maximum family income for the child tax credit would be $23,500. Why is the $300 prepayment not being sent to all these families? It would have been quite simple. Why discriminate on the basis of income?
We must also remember that this same Government lowered the ceiling for the child tax credit last year.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has done the same for the sales tax refund. However, as concerns the child tax credit, this would not cost the Government anything as it is already earmarked.
I trust that the one who replies will give me an answer this time. Let him tell us that, for the Conservatives, someone with a family income of $15,500 is now a wealthy person in Canada and that such a person will have to go to the tax discounters, the loan sharks, the friends of the Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Hon. Member, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Health and Welfare ... We haven't heard from him in a long time. Normally, it would be the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), better known now in Canada as the Minister of social injustice, who should have made sure that no one in Canada is penalized and that all taxpayers who receive the full child-tax credit get an early payment of $300 to ensure that these needy families . .. Also, this cheque should have been mailed in September and not in November, because it is when children are returning to school that their parents need the money.
Mr. Speaker, I dare hope I will get a favourable reply to this
question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: THE BUDGET-FAMILY INCOME STANDARDS. (B) REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), the child tax credit and the sales tax credit are two separate programs with different purposes. The child tax credit threshold of $23,500 in 1986 approximates the low-income cutoff point of a couple with three children in an intermediate size city. The average child tax credit family has 1.8 children, so the threshold is really quite generous. For exemple, for a couple with two children in an intermediate size city, the threshold is approximately $3,000 above the low-income cutoff point in 1986.
In the May 25, 1985, Budget, the threshold was reduced from $26,300 to $23,500 for the 1986 tax year and the credit value was substantially increased to $454 per child. The threshold will be indexed to the extent that inflation exceeds 3 per cent in order to help preserve its real value.
About 2.5 million families benefit from the child tax credit. The refundable sales tax credit will benefit over four million families and individuals, or about 40 per cent of all Canadian households. The federal sales tax credit is intended to protect the lowest income Canadians from the effect of the 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax. It will benefit many child tax credit families as well.
For example, the couple with two children and a net income of up to $18,000 will receive benefits. Obviously the Government cannot afford to give such a broad-based credit to every Canadian. Given limited resources, it was decided that a substantial credit to lower income families was a better use of public resources than a lower credit for a larger number of families. The credit will cost $330 million in 1986, which demonstrates the Government's real concern for low-income Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, you will remember as well as I do the frightening and astronomical interest rates of 1981. At that time mortgage rates were in excess of 20 per cent. It was those frightening and astronomical interest rates which brought on what has now been called the great recession of the 1980s. It was those interest rates which brought on record personal, corporate and farm bankruptcies. It was those interest rates which brought on unemployment that reached almost to 13 per cent of our entire workforce.
Despite the devastation which those interest rates wrought on our economy, and despite the havoc which they wreaked on the lives of individual ordinary Canadians, the Government of the day told us that it was impossible to bring down those interest rates because American interest rates were high. We were told that we could not bring down our interest rates below the American interest rates. Also, the Government of the day told us that if we did, we would have capital fleeing
