the country. We would have the dollar falling, we would have inflation rising, and we would have runaway inflation. In fact, the then Government said that our economy would be wrecked. Well, the economy was wrecked, not because of the falling dollar and the inflation situation, but because of those very high interest rates about which you, Mr. Speaker, and I and every Canadian was most concerned and crying for relief from.
Fortunately when the Conservative Government took office, we followed what I consider to be a low interest rate policy, either by good luck or good management. I choose to think that it has been through deliberate good management that interest rates have continued to fall with one or two modest exceptions. Sometimes, I must admit, when I hear comments from the Governor of the Bank of Canada, I shudder and think perhaps it is good luck rather than good management. However, by and large, I am sure that it is because of good management that interest rates have been falling.
As I indicated, there have been one or two exceptions. One of those exceptions occurred just last month when suddenly, as a result of our falling exchange rate, the Bank of Canada raised its lending rate, raised interest rates in Canada in order to do what was described as "burn the speculators" and to try to steady our Canadian dollar.
The result of our general over-all policy of falling interest rates had been good for the Canadian economy. We have seen unemployment fall. We have seen bankruptcies fall. We have seen the Gross National Product go up. We have seen housing starts go up. We have seen all economic indicators go up. Be that as it may, however, Canadian interest rates have continued to be above American interest rates. In spite of the rising economy and all other good indicators, we have seen the Canadian dollar continue to fall. However, with that falling dollar we have not seen the cost of living go up, we have not seen runaway inflation, and we have not seen the economy in a state of complete collapse, the way the former Government predicted. In fact, we have seen just the opposite. Be all that as it may, we still have an interest rate which is substantially above American interest rates. At the moment our prime rates are some 4 per cent above the American prime rate. Do we need an interest rate that high to keep our dollar steady and to support it? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker, and neither does the former adviser to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), Mr. William Mackness, who has recently been quoted inthe press as saying:
-the Government made a "major policy error" by going into the Budget with Canadian interest rates substantially higher than those in the United States.
Such a wide variation in interest rates is a source of instability in the Canadian dollar itself.
When interest rates are so far apart, you have to know something is seriously wrong. It's a little like someone trying to sell you a bond with a 25 per cent interest rate-you become suspicious of the product.
Mr. Mackness said that just a few days ago.
High interest rates obviously have not until recently been
doing anything for the Canadian dollar. In fact, it continued to
fall, which as been hurting our economy. The spread between the American interest rates and our own has had a serious effect on our economy. We must have low interest rates if we are to have a growing Gross National Product and if we are to have falling unemployment so that we can protect our social safety network.
Other countries have been dropping their interest rates lately. I hope that tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that at long last the Minister of Finance recognizes that our interest rates are too high in comparison with the American's and that they will start to come down. I trust the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that this very Thursday.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) raises a very important and interesting issue.
I would like to begin by suggesting that it is possible to have both lower interest rates and a stronger dollar. Indeed, the two go hand in hand.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
I believe that the policies which best promote this result, on a sustainable basis, are those designed to encourage non-inflationary growth. I think that is important. On the fiscal side, this involves the policy of sound financial management, including progressive reductions in the budget deficit, as emphasized in last month's Budget.
I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that there cannot be misgivings in financial markets about our commitment to a sound currency if we are to achieve lower interest rates and the foundation for the dollar is to be a firm one. That is why the authorities had to move in a forceful way recently to stem speculative excesses in the foreign exchange market. If these had been allowed to gather additional momentum, they could have spilled over into even stronger pressures on interest rates. I am sure the Hon. Member would agree with me on that.
While it is unfortunate, the route to sustainably lower interest rates inevitably involves some temporary reversals. 1 am convinced that to have attempted to avoid increases in interest rates through monetary means when the dollar was under strong downward pressure would have been self-defeating. The confidence of Canadian and foreign investors alike would have been undermined, in my estimation. The downward pressure on the dollar would have intensified, a strong risk of reversing the progress that has been made against inflation would have been run, and, ultimately, higher rather than lower Canadian interest rates would have resulted.
By acting as they did, Mr. Speaker, the authorities have paved the way for eventual interest rate declines, and I am sure you are going to see that happen.
The Canadian economy has performed, and I think the Hon. Member will agree with me, extremely well over the past 18 months. I can see the Hon. Member nodding his head. In 1985 our growth rate exceeded those of the United States and
March 11, 1986

Europe. That is important. Our prospects for this year continue to be favourable. The economic policies of this Government are providing the framework to ensure the recovery is not only sustained, but supported by low interest rates and a sound currency.
